docs.title: Attestation Standard vs Reporting Standard
docs.text: Category Attestation Standard Reporting Standard Definition A framework that governs how a practitioner (e.g., auditor) performs an attestation engagement — where they evaluate and provide assurance on a subject matter based on someone else’s assertion. A framework that governs how the results of an engagement are communicated — including format, content, and required disclosures in the final report. Example SSAE 18 is an attestation standard used for SOC 1 & SOC 2 reports. The structure of a SOC 1 & SOC 2 report (sections like management assertion, system description, auditor’s opinion). Focus Methodology, independence, evidence gathering, and assurance level. Presentation, clarity, and completeness of the report. Used For SOC reports, financial forecasts, compliance reviews, etc. Audit reports, SOC reports, financial statements, etc.

docs.title: End-to-End Audit & Certification Lifecycle (Step by Step)
docs.text:
This flow applies to any management system certification (ISO 27001, ISO 9001, etc.).

  • Gap assessment
  • System design & implementation
  • Audit readiness assessment
  • Internal audit & management review
  • Stage 1
  • Stage 2
  • Surveillance & recertification

docs.title: 1. Gap Assessment
docs.text:
Where are we today vs the standard?

Objective: Establish a baseline by comparing current practices against the requirements.

Activities & Outputs: Review policies, benchmark against clauses, identify gaps.

Deliverables include gap analysis report, risk register and remediation plan.

Key Point: 🚫 Not an audit — it’s strategic input for planning.

docs.title: 2. Design & Implement the Management System
docs.text:
Build what’s missing and fix what’s weak

Objective: Embed controls and close identified gaps.

Activities & Outputs: Define scope, perform risk assessments, write policies, implement processes, train staff, and generate records.

Deliverables include documented system, operating controls and compliance evidence.

Key Point: You cannot audit something that doesn’t exist — this step creates the system.

docs.title: 3. Audit Readiness Assessment
docs.text:
Are we actually ready to face an auditor?

Objective: Ensure preparedness before external audit.

Activities & Outputs: Conduct a mock audit, review documents, interview staff, test controls, validate evidence. Deliverables include pre audit checklist, findings, and corrective action plan.

Key Point: ✅ Confidence check before spending audit money.

docs.title: 4. Internal Audit
docs.text:
Are we complying with our own system?

Objective: Verify conformity and effectiveness internally.

Activities & Outputs: Audit against ISO clauses, collect evidence, raise nonconformities.

Deliverables include audit report and corrective actions.

Key Point: ✅ Mandatory before Stage 1 — cannot be skipped.

docs.title: 5. Management Review
docs.text:
Does leadership accept and support the system?

Objective: Demonstrate top management accountability.

Activities & Outputs: Review audit results, risks, incidents, metrics, and improvement opportunities.

Deliverables include meeting minutes and action items.

Key Point: Auditors will ask for proof this happened.

docs.title: 6. Stage 1 Audit
docs.text:
Is the system designed correctly and ready?

Objective: External auditor reviews documentation and readiness.

Activities & Outputs: Assess scope, documentation, risk approach, regulatory awareness, and completion of internal audit & management review.

Deliverables include Stage 1 audit report and readiness confirmation.

Key Point: Entry clearance to Stage 2.

docs.title: 7. Stage 2 Audit
docs.text:
Does the system actually work in real life?

Objective: Verify implementation and effectiveness.

Activities & Outputs: Observe processes, interview staff, review evidence, test controls, assess continual improvement.

Deliverables include Stage 2 audit findings.

Key Point: Certification decision depends on this stage.

docs.title: 8. Certification Decision
docs.text:
Objective: Approve or reject certification.

Activities & Outputs: Independent review of audit results, verification of corrective actions, issuance of certificate (valid 3 years).

Key Point: 🎯 The formal recognition of compliance.

docs.title: 9. Ongoing Compliance
docs.text:
Surveillance & Recertification

Objective: Maintain certification over time.

Activities & Outputs: Annual surveillance audits focusing on high risk areas, system changes, incidents, and leadership reviews. Every 3 years, a full recertification audit is conducted.

Key Point: Certification is maintained, not permanent.

docs.title: Main stages of Audit
docs.text:
1. Audit Planning

Purpose: Set the direction before any Audit begins.

  • Define audit objectives and scope

  • Identify criteria (laws, standards, policies)

  • Assess risks and key focus areas

  • Create the audit plan and schedule

  • Assign auditors and responsibilities

2. Audit Preparation

Purpose: Get ready to audit efficiently.

  • Review background documents and prior audits

  • Develop audit checklists and questions

  • Notify auditees and confirm logistics

  • Prepare sampling methods and tools

3. Opening Meeting

Purpose: Align expectations with the auditee.

  • Introduce the audit team

  • Confirm scope, objectives, and timetable

  • Explain audit methods and communication rules

  • Clarify roles and answer questions

4. Audit Execution (Fieldwork)

Purpose: Collect objective evidence.

  • Conduct interviews

  • Review documents and records

  • Observe processes and activities

  • Test controls and transactions

  • Record findings and evidence

This is where most of the audit effort happens.

5. Audit Analysis & Evaluation

Purpose: Decide what the evidence means.

  • Compare evidence against audit criteria

  • Identify:

    • Conformities
    • Nonconformities
    • Observations
    • Opportunities for improvement

  • Assess severity and root causes

6. Closing Meeting

Purpose: Communicate results clearly.

  • Present audit findings

  • Explain nonconformities and evidence

  • Discuss next steps and timelines

  • Ensure findings are understood (not debated)

7. Audit Reporting

Purpose: Provide the official audit record.

  • Prepare the audit report

  • Summarize scope, methodology, and findings

  • Include conclusions and recommendations

  • Distribute to relevant stakeholders

8. Corrective Actions & Follow-Up

Purpose: Make sure issues are fixed.

  • Auditee develops corrective action plans

  • Root cause analysis performed

  • Actions implemented and documented

  • Auditor verifies effectiveness (follow-up audit or review)

docs.title: Audit and Risk Management: First, Second, and Third Party Audits
docs.text: In audit and risk management, “first party,” “second party,” and “third party” describe the relationship between the auditor and the organization being audited — and they each serve different purposes in governance, compliance, and assurance.

docs.title: First-Party Audit – Internal Audit
docs.text:
Who conducts it: - Your own organization’s internal audit team - Staff independent of the area being audited

Purpose: - Verify compliance with internal policies, procedures, and standards - Identify gaps and opportunities for improvement before external scrutiny

Example: Your company’s internal audit department reviews IT access controls against your own security policy.

Risk Management Role: Early detection of issues; supports continuous improvement and readiness for external audits.

docs.title: Second-Party Audit – Supplier / Customer Audit
docs.text:
Who conducts it: - One organization audits another with which it has a direct contractual relationship - Often a customer auditing a supplier

Purpose: - Ensure the supplier meets contractual, quality, and compliance requirements - Verify specific controls or processes important to the buyer

Example: A manufacturer audits its parts supplier to ensure compliance with agreed production standards and delivery timelines.

Risk Management Role: Reduces supply chain risk by validating that partners meet agreed standards.

docs.title: Third-Party Audit – Independent / Certification Audit
docs.text:
Who conducts it: - An independent external body with no vested interest in either party - Examples: accredited certification bodies, regulators

Purpose: - Provide objective assurance that an organization meets a recognized standard or regulation (e.g., ISO 27001, PCI DSS) - Often results in formal certification or regulatory compliance status

Example: An accredited ISO registrar audits your company’s information security management system for certification.

Risk Management Role: Builds credibility and trust with customers, regulators, and stakeholders; validates compliance to external standards.

Note

The distinction between first, second, and third party audits lies in the relationship between the auditor and the organization. - First party: Internal, self-assessment. - Second party: Contractual, customer–supplier. - Third party: Independent, certification or regulatory assurance.

docs.title: Business Continuity Management System (BCMS)
docs.text: A pandemic, war, cyber-attack, natural disaster, or fire can all have a huge impact on a business. BCMS helps to restore normal business operations as quickly as possible, in times of crisis.

docs.title: Business Impact Analysis (BIA)
docs.text: An important part of the BCMS is the Business Impact Analysis (BIA), which identifies essential processes for your organisation and examines their availability requirements. The BIA should determine the operational and financial impacts of disruptions.

docs.title: Guide to Conducting a BIA
docs.text:
1. Identify Scope – Focus on the most critical departments or units. Select knowledgeable staff for interviews.
  2. Establish Value with Management – Ensure leadership understands the importance of BIA.
  3. Schedule & Prepare Interviews – Meet with department leaders and SMEs, ensuring they understand objectives and preparation needs.
  4. Execute BIA & Risk Assessment Interviews – Document activities, dependencies (applications, facilities, suppliers, equipment, personnel, interdependencies), downtime impacts, and peak times.
  5. Analyse Data & Identify Scenarios – Consider disruptions such as facility damage, equipment failure, supply chain interruptions, utility outages, IT/data loss, or staff absenteeism.
  6. Clarify Impacts – Quantify effects like lost sales, increased expenses, fines, penalties, customer loss, and delayed plans.
  7. Define Recovery Objectives – Establish RTO (maximum downtime tolerated), RPO (maximum data loss tolerated), and MTPD (maximum tolerable period of disruption). Use these to design disaster recovery and continuity plans, budgets, and capabilities.

docs.title: BIA Findings & Report
docs.text:
Present findings to leadership, including:

  • Executive summary (scope, objectives, methodology, impact measurement)
  • Process criticality ranking and recovery timeframes
  • Dependencies and compliance obligations
  • Risk exposure areas
  • Action plans (short, medium and long-term)
  • Supporting details (process data, participants, IT recovery categories, historical data)

docs.title: Implications of not performing a BIA
docs.text:
• Subjective Recovery Objectives & Confusion – Without a formal BIA, recovery priorities may be inconsistent across departments, leading to misaligned investments and unclear objectives.
  • Capability Gaps & Inaccurate Scope – Without top-down scoping, strategies may under or over-prepare, causing inefficiencies and gaps in continuity capabilities.
  • Lack of Investment Justification – Without BIA data, it’s difficult to justify preparedness spending to management.

docs.title: 1. Recovery Objectives
docs.text:
• Recovery Time Objective (RTO): How quickly critical processes were restored after a disruption.
  • Recovery Point Objective (RPO): How much data loss (in time) was experienced vs. the target.
  • Work Recovery Time (WRT): Time needed after systems are restored to validate data, check integrity, and bring business processes fully back online.
  • Example: Restoring a database may take 2 hours (RTO), but reconciling transactions may take another 1 hour (WRT).
  • Maximum Tolerable Downtime or Period of Disruption (MTD/MTPD): The total maximum time a business process can be unavailable before causing irreparable harm (financial, reputational, regulatory).
  • Formula: MTD = RTO + WRT.

docs.title: 2. Incident & Response Metrics
docs.text:
• Incident Response Time: Average time taken to activate the BC plan after an incident.
  • Emergency Response Time: Time to initiate emergency procedures (e.g., evacuation, crisis call tree).
  • Incident Identification & Reporting: Time taken to detect and report disruptions.

docs.title: 3. Testing & Exercising
docs.text:
• Plan Testing Effectiveness: % of successful BC/DR tests vs. planned.
  • Frequency of Tests: Number of continuity exercises conducted per year.
  • Lessons Learned Closure Rate: % of corrective actions from tests/incidents closed on time.

docs.title: 4. Awareness & Training
docs.text:
• Employee Training Coverage: % of staff trained in BCMS roles and responsibilities.
  • Awareness Levels: Survey scores or participation rates in awareness campaigns.

docs.title: 5. Resource & Supply Chain Resilience
docs.text:
• Critical Resource Availability: % uptime of essential systems, facilities, or staff.
  • Supplier Recovery Performance: % of critical suppliers meeting their continuity SLAs.

docs.title: 6. Compliance & Audit
docs.text:
• Audit Findings: Number of nonconformities or observations in BCMS audits.
  • Compliance Rate: % adherence to ISO 22301 or internal BCMS requirements.

docs.title: 7. Business Impact
docs.text:
• Cost of Disruption: Financial losses per incident vs. acceptable thresholds.
  • Customer/Stakeholder Satisfaction: Feedback on continuity performance during/after incidents.

docs.title: Business Impact Analysis (BIA) vs Risk Assessment
docs.text:
• Risk Assessment – Identifies threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood, and impact; includes a treatment plan.
  • Business Impact Analysis – Focuses on the consequences of disruptions to critical processes and the speed of recovery needed to avoid severe damage.
Feature Business Impact Analysis (BIA) Risk Assessment Focus Impact of disruptions on business operations Likelihood and severity of threats and vulnerabilities Goal Identify critical functions and recovery priorities Identify and evaluate risks to mitigate them Output Recovery Time Objectives (RTO), Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) Risk levels, mitigation strategies When Used During business continuity planning During security planning and compliance

docs.title: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), 2020
docs.text: The California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) is a data privacy law enacted in the U.S. state of California. It was designed to give California residents greater control over their personal information held by businesses.

docs.title: Purpose of CCPA
docs.text:
• Enhance consumer privacy rights
  • Increase transparency in how personal data is collected, used, and shared
  • Hold businesses accountable for data protection and disclosure

docs.title: Key Rights for California Consumers
docs.text:
Under the CCPA, California residents have the right to:

Right Description Right to Access Request a copy of the personal data collected Right to Know What personal data is collected, used, shared, or sold Right to Delete Request deletion of personal data held by businesses Right to Opt-Out Say no to the sale of personal information Right to Non-Discrimination Not be penalized for exercising privacy rights

docs.title: Who Must Comply
docs.text:
The CCPA applies to for-profit businesses that:

  • Have annual gross revenue over $25 million USD
  • Buy, receive, or sell personal data of 100,000+ consumers or households
  • Earn 50% or more of annual revenue from selling personal data

Businesses do not need to be based in California — if they serve California residents and meet the criteria, they must comply.

docs.title: The CCPA, as Amended by the CPRA
docs.text:
In 2020, voters approved the California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA), which amended and strengthened the CCPA:

  • Added new rights (e.g., correction of personal data)
  • Created the California Privacy Protection Agency for enforcement
  • Tightened rules for sensitive personal information

docs.title: Enforcement and Penalties ⚠️
docs.text:
• Enforced by: California Attorney General and the California Privacy Protection Agency
  • Civil penalties: Up to $2,500 per unintentional violation and $7,500 per intentional violation
  • Consumer lawsuits: Individuals can sue for certain data breaches, with statutory damages between $100 and $750 per incident

docs.title: CERT-In Directions, 2022
docs.text: India Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) is India’s national incident response mandate.

docs.title: Applicability
docs.text:
• Service providers
  • Data centers
  • Intermediaries
  • Corporates
  • Government organizations

docs.title: Key Provisions
docs.text:
• Mandatory 6-hour breach reporting
  • Time synchronization
  • Logs retention for 180 days
  • Subscriber information retention for at least 5 years

docs.title: Compliance Expectations
docs.text:
• Reporting - Any cybersecurity incidents or breaches must be reported within 6 hours.
  • Operations - Systems must time-sync with NIC/NPL NTP; maintain logs and supply information in formats/timelines specified by CERT-In when directed.
    • NIC (National Informatics Centre): Operates multiple NTP servers (such as samay1.nic.in and samay2.nic.in) to provide synchronized time across government networks.
    • NPL (National Physical Laboratory): The custodian of Indian Standard Time (IST), maintaining the "Primary Timescale" traceable to global Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Its NTP server is time.nplindia.org

NIC and NPL refer to the two primary government bodies that provide official time synchronization services for India's digital infrastructure.

docs.title: Penalties
docs.text:
• Directions are legally enforceable under the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000. The agency has the statutory authority to issue binding directions for carrying out its cybersecurity functions
  • When non-compliance is found to be deliberate, 1 year imprisonment or 1 lakh fine or both can be imposed
  • The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Bill, 2023 proposed raising the maximum fine upto to ₹1 crore.

docs.title: PACT
docs.text:
Platform for Automated Cybersecurity Threat intelligence (PACT)

  • PACT is a government initiative under MeitY to automate cyber threat intelligence sharing.
  • It aggregates threat data from multiple sources and provides actionable intelligence to organizations.
  • Helps India build a collaborative cyber defense ecosystem.
  • While CERT-In references PACT in its initiatives, there is no standalone public-facing portal yet. Updates are usually published through MeitY and CERT-In announcements.

External link: cert-in and cert-in cyber alerts

docs.title: CIS’s - Critical Security Controls
docs.text: Developed by the Centre for Internet Security, the CIS Controls are a prioritized, prescriptive set of 18 safeguards that address the most common cyberthreats. Formerly known as SANS 20.

docs.title: Summary of the 18 controls
docs.text:
1. Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets: Managing all hardware devices connected to the infrastructure for monitoring and protection.

  2. Inventory and Control of Software Assets: Managing all software on the network, ensuring only authorized software is used.

  3. Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software: Maintaining secure settings for all assets and software.

  4. Account Management: Managing user account credentials and authorizations.

  5. Access Control Management: Managing access credentials and privileges for all accounts.

  6. Audit Log Management: Collecting, alerting on, reviewing, and retaining audit logs to aid in detecting and recovering from attacks.

  7. Data Protection: Identifying, classifying, and securely handling data throughout its lifecycle.

  8. Data Recovery: Establishing practices to restore assets to a trusted state after an incident.

  9. Incident Response Management: Establishing a program to prepare for, detect, and respond to security incidents.

  10. Email and Web Browser Protections: Enhancing protections against threats originating from email and web browsing.

  11. Continuous Vulnerability Management: Regularly assessing and remediating vulnerabilities on all assets.

  12. Malware Defence: Preventing the installation and execution of malicious code on enterprise assets.

  13. Network Infrastructure Management: Securely managing network devices to prevent exploitation.

  14. Network Monitoring and Defence: Maintaining comprehensive network monitoring to defend against threats.

  15. Application Software Security: Managing the security of software throughout its lifecycle.

  16. Penetration Testing: Testing the effectiveness of security controls by simulating attacker actions.

  17. Security Awareness and Skills Training: Implementing a program to educate the workforce on security best practices.

  18. Service Provider Management: Evaluating service providers to ensure they adequately protect sensitive data and critical platforms.

docs.title: Three implementation Groups
docs.text:
The CIS Controls are structured into three Implementation Groups (IGs 1-3) to accommodate organizations of different sizes and with different resources.

• IG1 (Basic Cyber Hygiene): This group consists of 56 Safeguards and represents the minimum standard of information security for all enterprises. It focuses on essential practices to defend against the most common attacks.

• IG2: Building upon IG1, this group adds 74 Safeguards, addressing a wider range of threats and vulnerabilities and suitable for organizations with moderate complexity.

• IG3: This group encompasses all 153 Safeguards, offering comprehensive protection against advanced threats and designed for larger organizations with significant resources and expertise.

docs.title: COBIT (Control Objectives for Information and related Technologies)
docs.text:
COBIT, developed by ISACA, is an IT governance and management framework that aligns IT processes with business goals, optimizes resource use, and provides metrics for performance and risk management. COBIT 2019 organizes its governance system into five domains, each containing processes that represent key activities for managing and governing enterprise IT. These domains are split between Governance Objectives and Management Objectives.

Five COBIT Domains and Their Process Groups

Domain Type Purpose EDM (Evaluate, Direct and Monitor) Governance Ensures stakeholder needs are evaluated, direction is set, and performance is monitored. APO (Align, Plan and Organize) Management Covers strategy, governance, and planning of IT. BAI (Build, Acquire and Implement) Management Focuses on implementation and integration of IT solutions. DSS (Deliver, Service and Support) Management Manages operational delivery of IT services. MEA (Monitor, Evaluate and Assess) Management Evaluates performance, compliance, and internal controls.

docs.title: Governance Domain
docs.text:
EDM – Evaluate, Direct and Monitor

Purpose: Provide board-level oversight to ensure IT delivers value, optimizes risk, and uses resources responsibly. Focuses on strategic oversight and decision-making.

Expand for the table Process Purpose Statement EDM01 Ensure Governance Framework Setting and Maintenance EDM02 Ensure Benefits Delivery EDM03 Ensure Risk Optimization EDM04 Ensure Resource Optimization EDM05 Ensure Stakeholder Engagement

Each EDM process includes:

• Purpose Statement: Why the process exists.

• Process Practices: Key activities to perform. e.g., define governance principles, monitor performance.

• Inputs/Outputs: Artifacts consumed and produced. E.g. governance policies, performance reports.

• Goals & Metrics: stakeholder satisfaction, risk posture.

• Governance Components: organizational structures, principles, policies.

docs.title: Management Domains
docs.text:
1.APO – Align, Plan and Organize

Purpose: Translate enterprise strategy and risk appetite into a coherent IT management framework and roadmap. Strategic planning, risk management, and resource alignment.

Expand for the table Process Purpose Statement APO01 Manage the IT Management Framework APO02 Manage Strategy APO03 Manage Enterprise Architecture APO04 Manage Innovation APO05 Manage Portfolio APO06 Manage Budget and Costs APO07 Manage Human Resources APO08 Manage Relationships APO09 Manage Service Agreements APO10 Manage Suppliers APO11 Manage Quality APO12 Manage Risk APO13 Manage Security

2.BAI – Build, Acquire and Implement

Purpose: Deliver new and changed IT solutions into operation securely and efficiently. Development, acquisition, and deployment of IT solutions.

Expand for the table Process Purpose Statement BAI01 Manage Programs and Projects BAI02 Manage Requirements Definition BAI03 Manage Solutions Identification and Build BAI04 Manage Availability and Capacity BAI05 Manage Organizational Change Enablement BAI06 Manage Changes BAI07 Manage Change Acceptance and Transitioning BAI08 Manage Knowledge BAI09 Manage Assets BAI10 Manage Configuration

3.DSS – Deliver, Service and Support

Purpose: Operate and support IT services securely, meeting agreed levels and responding to incidents. Operational delivery and support of IT services.

Expand for the table Process Purpose Statement DSS01 Manage Operations DSS02 Manage Service Requests and Incidents DSS03 Manage Problems DSS04 Manage Continuity DSS05 Manage Security Services DSS06 Manage Business Process Controls

4.MEA – Monitor, Evaluate and Assess Purpose: Provide assurance through monitoring performance, conformance, and compliance. Performance monitoring, compliance, and internal control.

Expand for the table Process Purpose Statement MEA01 Monitor, Evaluate and Assess Performance and Conformance MEA02 Monitor, Evaluate and Assess the System of Internal Control MEA03 Monitor, Evaluate and Assess Compliance with External Requirements

Governance Components in COBIT

Each process is supported by seven governance components:

  1. Processes

  2. Organizational Structures

  3. Information

  4. Culture, Ethics and Behavior

  5. People, Skills and Competencies

  6. Services, Infrastructure and Applications

  7. Policies and Procedures

These components ensure that each process is actionable, measurable, and aligned with enterprise goals. Goals and Metrics. COBIT uses performance management based on CMMI-like maturity levels - from Level 0 (Incomplete) to Level 5 (Optimizing).

docs.title: COSO Framework (Internal Control – Integrated Framework)
docs.text:
• Developed by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO). It was first introduced in 1992 and updated in 2013.

  • Provides a broad, principles-based framework for designing, implementing, and evaluating internal controls.

  • Built around 5 components (Control Environment, Risk Assessment, Control Activities, Information & Communication, Monitoring) and 17 principles.

Widely used for financial reporting, compliance, and enterprise risk management (e.g., SOX compliance).

docs.title: Relationship between COSO Framework and Common Criteria
1. The five Core Components of COSO
docs.text:
• Control Environment – Ethical tone, governance, and accountability culture.

  • Control Activities – Policies and procedures to mitigate risks.

  • Risk Assessment – Identifying and analysing risks to objectives.

  • Information & Communication – Sharing relevant, timely information internally and externally.

  • Monitoring Activities – Ongoing evaluation of control effectiveness.

docs.title: 2. Common Criteria (SOC 2 – Trust Services Criteria)
docs.text:
• Defined by the AICPA for System and Organization Controls (SOC 2) reporting.

  • Focuses on security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.

  • The Common Criteria are the baseline requirements that apply across all Trust Services Categories (TSC) and then and then each category (Security, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Availability & Privacy) has additional criteria layered on top.

  • They are more specific to IT systems, service organizations, and SaaS providers.

docs.title: 3. How They Connect
docs.text:
• The AICPA Trust Services Criteria (Common Criteria) are explicitly aligned with COSO.

  • COSO provides the foundational internal control principles, while the Common Criteria adapt those principles to IT and service organization contexts.

  • For example:

    • COSO Principle: Control Environment → Common Criteria: Commitment to integrity, ethical values, and competence.

    • COSO Principle: Risk Assessment → Common Criteria: Identifying and assessing risks to system objectives.

docs.title: Mandatory: Common Criteria (CC) for TSC
docs.text:
CC1: Control Environment: Defines the organization's ethical values, integrity, and commitment to oversight.

CC2: Communication and Information: Addresses how organization communicate policies, procedures, and responsibilities to staff and external parties.

CC3: Risk Assessment: Covers how organization identifies and analyzes risks to its objectives.

CC4: Monitoring Activities: Ensures org has procedures to track and evaluate the effectiveness of controls over time.

CC5: Control Activities: Refers to the specific controls and technologies you implement to mitigate risks.

CC6: Logical and Physical Access Controls: Governs how your organization restricts logical (e.g., user credentials) and physical (e.g., server rooms) access to its systems and assets.

CC7: System Operations: Focuses on detecting and responding to system issues, including incident management and vulnerability monitoring.

CC8: Change Management: Covers the authorization, testing, and implementation of system changes.

CC9: Risk Mitigation: Deals with mitigating risks arising from business partners, vendors, and internal changes.

docs.title: CC1: Control Environment
docs.text:
Focus: Governance, ethics, accountability, competence.

Sub-classifications include:

CC1.1 – Commitment to integrity and ethical values

CC1.2 – Board independence and oversight

CC1.3 – Establishes structure, authority, and responsibility

CC1.4 – Commitment to competence

CC1.5 – Accountability for internal control responsibilities

docs.title: CC2: Communication & Information
docs.text:
Focus: Internal and external communication of policies and responsibilities.

Sub-classifications include:

CC2.1 – Uses relevant, quality information

CC2.2 – Communicates internally

CC2.3 – Communicates externally

docs.title: CC3: Risk Assessment
docs.text:
Focus: Identifying and analyzing risks, including fraud and change.

Sub-classifications include:

CC3.1 – Specifies suitable objectives

CC3.2 – Identifies and analyzes risks

CC3.3 – Assesses fraud risk

CC3.4 – Identifies and analyzes significant change

docs.title: CC4: Monitoring of Controls
docs.text:
Focus: Ongoing and separate evaluations of control effectiveness.

Sub-classifications include:

CC4.1 – Conducts ongoing and/or separate evaluations

CC4.2 – Evaluates and communicates deficiencies

docs.title: CC5: Control Activities
docs.text:
Focus: Policies, procedures, and IT general controls.

Sub-classifications include:

CC5.1 – Selects and develops control activities

CC5.2 – Selects and develops general controls over technology

CC5.3 – Deploys control activities through policies and procedures

docs.title: CC6: Logical & Physical Access Controls
docs.text:
Focus: Restricting access to systems, data, and facilities.

Sub-classifications include:

CC6.1 – Logical access security software, infrastructure, and architectures

CC6.2 – Registration and authorization of new/internal users

CC6.3 – Removal of access when no longer authorized

CC6.4 – Authentication mechanisms (e.g., MFA)

CC6.5 – Restricting physical access to facilities

CC6.6 – Securing workstations, laptops, and mobile devices

CC6.7 – Encryption and protection of data in transit and at rest

docs.title: CC7: System Operations
docs.text:
Focus: Managing operations, detecting anomalies, incident response.

Sub-classifications include:

CC7.1 – Detects and monitors system components

CC7.2 – Identifies and logs anomalies

CC7.3 – Assesses security events and incidents

CC7.4 – Responds to and mitigates incidents

CC7.5 – Recovers from incidents and resumes operations

docs.title: CC8: Change Management
docs.text:
Focus: Controlling changes to infrastructure, applications, and data.

Sub-classifications include:

CC8.1 – Authorizes and documents changes

CC8.2 – Tests, approves, and implements changes

CC8.3 – Restricts emergency changes and documents them

CC8.4 – Maintains version control and rollback procedures

docs.title: CC9: Risk Mitigation
docs.text:
Focus: Managing risks from vendors, partners, and external parties.

Sub-classifications include:

CC9.1 – Identifies and assesses risks from business partners and vendors

CC9.2 – Implements risk mitigation strategies (e.g., contracts, monitoring)

CC9.3 – Reviews and updates risk mitigation activities periodically

Key Takeaway

  • CC1–CC5 = Broad governance and internal control principles (aligned with COSO).

  • CC6–CC9 = IT and operational safeguards (access, operations, change, vendor risk).

docs.title: AICPA Trust Services Criteria
docs.text: Additional criteria layered on top of each TSC (Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, Privacy), also referred as the AICPA Trust Services Criteria .

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
• Objective: Systems are available for operation and use as committed.
  • Criteria:
    • Common Criteria (CC1–CC9)
    • Additional Availability Criteria (A-Series):
      • A1.1: Availability commitments (e.g., uptime, SLAs)
      • A1.2: Backup and disaster recovery procedures
      • A1.3: Business continuity planning

docs.title: Confidentiality
docs.text:
• Objective: Information designated as confidential is protected.
  • Criteria:
    • Common Criteria (CC1–CC9)
    • Additional Confidentiality Criteria (C-Series):
      • C1.1: Identification and classification of confidential information
      • C1.2: Protection of confidential information during storage, transmission, and disposal.

docs.title: Processing Integrity
docs.text:
• Objective: System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely, and authorized.
  • Criteria:
    • Common Criteria (CC1–CC9)
    • Additional Processing Integrity Criteria (PI-Series):
      • PI1.1: Input data validation
      • PI1.2: Processing accuracy and completeness
      • PI1.3: Output accuracy and completeness
      • PI1.4: Timeliness of processing
      • PI1.5: Authorization of processing activities

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
• Objective: Personal information is collected, used, retained, disclosed, and disposed of in line with commitments and privacy principles (adapted from GAPP).
  • Note: Useful when Service Organization is a data controller.
  • Criteria:
    • Common Criteria (CC1–CC9)
    • Additional Privacy Criteria (P-Series):
      • P1.1: Notice and communication of privacy practices
      • P1.2: Choice and consent
      • P1.3: Collection of personal information
      • P1.4: Use, retention, and disposal
      • P1.5: Access to personal information
      • P1.6: Disclosure to third parties
      • P1.7: Security for privacy (overlaps with CC6)
      • P1.8: Quality and monitoring of personal information

docs.title: The Three Lines of Defence Model in Cybersecurity
docs.text: The Three Lines of Defence (3LoD) model in cybersecurity is a risk management framework that defines roles and responsibilities across three layers: operational, oversight, and assurance. It helps organizations manage cyber risks systematically.

docs.title: First Line: Operational Management
docs.text:
Who: - IT teams - System administrators - Network engineers - SOC analysts - Business unit managers

What They Do: - Implement security controls (e.g., firewalls, antivirus, access controls) - Monitor systems and respond to threats - Own and manage assets like data, applications, and infrastructure

Goal: Prevent and detect threats through day-to-day operations.

docs.title: Second Line: Risk Management & Compliance
docs.text:
Who: - Risk officers - Compliance teams - Cybersecurity governance staff

What They Do: - Develop policies, standards, and frameworks - Monitor adherence to regulations and internal controls - Provide guidance and oversight to the first line

Goal: Ensure risks are identified, assessed, and managed proactively.

docs.title: Third Line: Internal Audit
docs.text:
Who: - Internal auditors - Independent assurance teams

What They Do: - Evaluate the effectiveness of controls and risk management - Conduct audits and report findings to senior leadership - Provide independent assurance on the entire security posture

Goal: Validate that the first and second lines are functioning effectively.

Note

External audit is not considered the third line of defence in the standard Three Lines of Defence (3LoD) model. The third line consists of internal audit, which provides independent assurance on the effectiveness of the first (operational management) and second (risk/compliance functions) lines.

docs.title: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
docs.text: The Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA) is a European Union regulation designed to strengthen the ability of financial institutions to withstand and recover from ICT-related disruptions such as cyberattacks, system failures, or other digital risks.

docs.title: Key Facts About DORA
docs.text:
• Official Name: Regulation (EU) 2022/2554
  • Scope: Applies to banks, insurance companies, investment firms, payment institutions, and ICT third-party service providers
  • Goal: Ensure digital operational resilience across the EU financial sector by harmonizing rules and reducing vulnerabilities to cyber threats
  • Implementation Date: Entered into application on 17 January 2025

docs.title: Core Requirements Under DORA
docs.text:
• ICT Risk Management: Institutions must establish frameworks to identify, prevent, and mitigate ICT risks
  • Incident Reporting: Mandatory reporting of major ICT-related incidents to regulators within strict timeframes (e.g., initial notification often within 24 hours)
  • Digital Operational Resilience Testing: Required annual basic testing of ICT systems and, for critical entities, advanced Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT) every three years
  • Third-Party Risk Oversight: Actively manage risks from external vendors, including mandatory contractual clauses and exit strategies
  • Information Sharing: Participate in sharing cyber threat intelligence

docs.title: Enforcement and Penalties
docs.text:
Enforcement is handled by national competent authorities (such as the ECB or national regulators).

Non-compliance can result in:

  • Fines for Financial Entities: Up to 2% of global annual turnover
  • Fines for Critical ICT Providers: Up to 1% of average daily worldwide turnover, levied daily for up to six months until compliance is achieved
  • Personal Liability: Senior management can be held personally accountable for failures to implement required risk frameworks

docs.title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and Rules, 2025 (Consolidated)
1. Scope & Applicability
docs.text:
• Territorial Applies to processing in India and outside India if linked to goods/services offered to Indian individuals.
  • Material Covers digital personal data and digitized offline data.
  • Exemptions Domestic/personal use, publicly available data, certain government functions (security, sovereignty, public order), and research/statistical purposes (per Rules 2025).

docs.title: 2. Stakeholders
docs.text:
• Data Principals: Individuals whose data is processed.
  • Data Fiduciaries: Entities deciding purpose/means of processing.
  • Significant Data Fiduciaries (SDFs): Large-scale processors with extra obligations (DPO, audits, DPIA).
  • Data Processors: Process data on behalf of fiduciaries.
  • Consent Managers: Registered intermediaries to manage consent flows.
  • Data Protection Board of India: Regulator enforcing compliance, penalties, grievance redressal.

docs.title: 3. Grounds of Processing
docs.text:
• Consent: Free, specific, informed, unconditional, unambiguous, affirmative. Withdrawable anytime.
  • Legitimate Uses: Legal obligations, medical emergencies, employment, public interest, disaster response, etc.

docs.title: 4. Rights of Data Principals
docs.text:
• Access, correction, erasure (where consent is the ground).
  • Withdraw consent.
  • Grievance redressal (response within 90 days under Rules 2025).
  • Nomination rights (assign another person to exercise rights in case of death/incapacity).

docs.title: 5. Obligations of Data Fiduciaries
docs.text:
• Provide clear privacy notices (English or 22 Indian languages).
  • Implement safeguards (encryption, masking, monitoring, backups).
  • Establish grievance redressal mechanisms.
  • Delete data once purpose is fulfilled or consent withdrawn.
  • Notify breaches to Board and affected individuals.
  • Maintain contracts with Data Processors.

docs.title: Additional for SDFs
docs.text:
• Appoint DPO in India and independent data auditor.
  • Conduct annual audits & DPIAs.
  • Ensure algorithmic transparency.

docs.title: 6. Consent Managers
docs.text:
• Must register with the Data Protection Board.
  • Provide interoperable digital platforms for consent management.
  • Retain consent records for 7 years.
  • Cannot subcontract obligations or have conflicts of interest.
  • Subject to independent certification and audits.

docs.title: 7. Children’s Data
docs.text:
• Requires verifiable parental consent.
  • Prohibits tracking, behavioral monitoring, targeted advertising.
  • Exemptions: Schools, healthcare professionals, crèches, child transport providers.

docs.title: 8. Cross-Border Data Transfer
docs.text:
• Allowed unless restricted by the Central Government (blacklist approach).
  • SDFs must comply with restrictions on sensitive categories identified by government.

docs.title: 9. Breach Notification (Rules 2025)
docs.text:
• Primary intimation to Board: Without delay upon becoming aware.
  • Secondary intimation to Board: Within 72 hours with detailed information.
  • Notification to Data Principals: Without delay, including nature, impact, mitigation measures, and contact details.

docs.title: 10. Record Retention (Rules 2025)
docs.text:
• General Rule: Retain logs of processing transactions for at least 1 year.
  • Special Classes (E-commerce, Gaming, Social Media):
    • Data Fiduciaries in the following classes must retain personal data for only three years from the last time the Data Principal approached them:
      • E-commerce entities with at least 2 crore registered users in India
      • Online gaming intermediaries with at least 50 lakh registered users in India
      • Social media intermediaries with at least 2 crore registered users in India
    • Must notify Data Principals 48 hours before deletion.
  • Consent Managers: Retain consent records for 7 years.

docs.title: 11. Exemptions from Retention
docs.text:
• Certain classes of fiduciaries (e.g., healthcare providers, educational institutions, child transport providers) are exempt from strict parental consent obligations when processing children’s data.
  • Research, archiving, and statistical processing exempt if lawful, necessary, accurate, and safeguarded.

docs.title: 12. Penalties
docs.text:
• Data Fiduciaries: Up to ₹250 crore.
  • Breach of security safeguards: Up to ₹250 crore.
  • Breach of children’s data obligations: Up to ₹200 crore.
  • Breach of SDF obligations: Up to ₹150 crore.
  • Data Principals: Fine up to ₹10,000 for misuse of rights/frivolous complaints.
  • Consent Managers: Penalties for non-compliance.

docs.title: 13. Compliance Journey
docs.text:
1. Design privacy policies & procedures.
  2. Serve privacy notices at data collection points.
  3. Document legal grounds of processing.
  4. Obtain and manage consent (via Consent Manager if needed).
  5. Implement safeguards (encryption, monitoring, backups).
  6. Enable rights requests & grievance redressal.
  7. Maintain breach notification templates.
  8. Review Data Processor contracts.
  9. Erase personal data after purpose expiry.
  10. For SDFs: Appoint DPO, conduct DPIAs, audits.

docs.title: Nov 2025 – May 2026 (0–6 months after notification)
docs.text:
• Develop/refresh data privacy framework.
  • Draft and publish privacy notices (categories of data, purposes, withdrawal mechanisms, grievance process).
  • Conduct data mapping (repositories, flows, recipients).
  • Implement baseline security safeguards (encryption, access controls, log monitoring, backups, DR/BCP).
  • Update contracts with third parties to include privacy obligations.
  • Establish breach response procedures (notify Board + Data Principals without undue delay).
  • Launch data privacy training programs.
  • Define data retention procedures (logs retained ≥1 year, 3 year retention schedule for special classes).

docs.title: May – Nov 2026 (6–12 months)
docs.text:
• Establish mechanisms for:
    • Annual Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs).
    • Independent annual audits.
    • Algorithmic transparency & fairness assessments.
  • Prepare for potential data localisation requirements.
  • Implement Privacy Enabling Technologies (PETs) for automation.
  • Undertake external certifications (e.g., Privacy Information Management System – PIMS).

docs.title: Nov 2026 – May 2027 (Beyond 12–18 months)
docs.text:
Full compliance with remaining Rules:

  • Consent Manager registration & obligations (Rule 4).
  • Children’s data obligations (verifiable parental consent, exemptions for schools/healthcare).
  • Processing of data for persons with disabilities (guardian consent verification).
  • Additional obligations for Significant Data Fiduciaries (SDFs) (DPO, audits, DPIAs).
  • Cross border transfer compliance (Rule 15).
  • Research/statistical exemptions (Rule 16).
  • Rights of Data Principals (Rule 14).
  • Appeals to Appellate Tribunal (Rule 22).

docs.title: Key points
docs.text:
Redudancy vs Disaster Recovery

  • Redundancy duplicates critical elements like servers, power supplies, or network paths to eliminate single points of failure and ensure continuous operation during minor faults. Disaster recovery involves strategies, backups, and procedures to restore data and services following catastrophic events such as cyberattacks or natural disasters.

  • Redundancy aims for high availability with minimal or no interruption via active failover, often within the same site. Disaster recovery targets full restoration after widespread outages, potentially using offsite replicas, and accepts longer recovery times.

  • Load balancing distributes incoming traffic evenly across redundant servers or instances, ensuring no single point overloads and maintaining uptime during component failures. This supports redundancy by leveraging duplicated resources, such as multiple servers in a cluster, for seamless operation. Load balancers route traffic to secondary sites or regions post-disaster, using health checks to detect and failover from failed zones automatically. Global load balancers extend this across regions, minimizing RTO by switching to available backups quickly.

docs.title: Hot Site vs Cold Site
docs.text:
A hot site is a fully equipped backup facility that can take over operations almost immediately after a disaster, while a cold site is just a basic space with minimal infrastructure, requiring significant time and setup before it becomes operational.

A cold site it has technology at a minimal level. People (trained staff) and processes (detailed recovery procedures) must be brought in during activation, as the site arrives empty and requires significant setup time.

Feature Hot Site Cold Site Definition A continuously running backup site ready to take over operations instantly. A bare facility with basic infrastructure but no active systems. Setup Time Minimal — operations can resume within hours or less. Long — may take days or weeks to become functional. Infrastructure Fully equipped with hardware, software, networking, and internet connectivity. Only physical space, power, and cooling; equipment must be brought in. Data Availability Data is continuously replicated or backed up to the site. No real-time data; requires manual restoration from backups. Cost High (due to constant maintenance and readiness). Low (minimal ongoing costs). Use Case Mission-critical businesses needing near-zero downtime (banks, hospitals, e-commerce). Organizations with less critical operations that can tolerate downtime.

docs.title: Cold Site Limitations
docs.text:
• Provides only the physical environment (building, power, cooling).
  • Requires transporting servers, installing software, and restoring data before use.
  • Suitable for organizations with lower disaster recovery budgets or less critical workloads.

docs.title: Trade-Offs
docs.text:
• Cost vs. Speed is the main difference:
  • Hot sites are expensive but fast.
  • Cold sites are cheap but slow.
  • Many companies adopt a hybrid approach (warm site) to balance cost and recovery time.

docs.title: Risks & Considerations
docs.text:
• Hot Site: High cost may be unjustifiable for small businesses unless downtime is catastrophic.
  • Cold Site: Risk of prolonged downtime and potential data loss if backups are not current.
  • Decision Point: Evaluate Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO).
  • Hot sites excel at tight RTO/RPO.
  • Cold sites do not.

docs.title: Hot Site vs Mirror Site
docs.text:
A hot site is a disaster recovery facility that is fully operational and ready to take over business functions immediately after a failure. A mirror site, on the other hand, is an exact replica of a website or system, often used to distribute traffic, reduce latency, or provide redundancy.

Feature Hot Site Mirror Site Purpose Disaster recovery and business continuity Load balancing, redundancy, and faster access Scope Entire IT infrastructure (servers, apps, data, networking) Primarily websites or data repositories Activation Used only during disasters or outages Active all the time, serving users simultaneously Data Sync Data replicated regularly to ensure minimal downtime Data mirrored in real-time or near real-time Cost High (requires full infrastructure and maintenance) Moderate (depends on hosting and bandwidth) Use Case Banks, hospitals, airlines needing instant failover Large websites, software repositories, or global services like Wikipedia/CDNs

docs.title: Risks & Considerations
docs.text:
• Hot Site: Very expensive to maintain; only justified for mission-critical operations.
  • Mirror Site: Needs constant synchronization; if not properly managed, users may encounter outdated or inconsistent data. Performance overhead may occur if replication isn’t optimized.
  • Alternative Approaches: Some organizations use active-active clusters or geo-redundant architectures instead of a simple mirror site, achieving the same goals with more flexibility.

docs.title: Enterprise Architecture (EA)
docs.text:
It refers to the strategic design and alignment of an organization's security policies, processes, technologies, and people to support business objectives while protecting information assets.

Enterprise Security Architecture (ESA) is a subset of EA that specifically focuses on integrating security throughout the entire organizational structure, ensuring that security measures are neither isolated nor afterthoughts, but rather embedded into the foundational business strategy.

The primary purpose of enterprise security architecture is to establish alignment between business strategy and IT security operations. Without this alignment, security investments may not deliver value to the organization, and business initiatives may proceed without adequate protection. ESA provides the framework through which organizations can systematically design, construct, and maintain security strategies that both protect assets and enable business operations.

Most Commonly Used Frameworks

docs.title: 1. SABSA (Sherwood Applied Business Security Architecture)
docs.text:
SABSA is a business-driven, top-down security architecture methodology that emphasizes developing security from the perspective of business requirements rather than starting with technical controls. It structures security architecture through six distinct layers, each answering specific questions about the security architecture:

The six layers

Contextual Architecture (Why?): Analyzes the business context, mission, strategy, policies, and risks to understand why security is needed. This layer examines business drivers, threats, and opportunities that shape security requirements.

Conceptual Architecture (What?): Identifies critical business assets, information, and systems requiring protection. This layer defines the security attributes needed to support business objectives (such as confidentiality, integrity, availability, and accountability).

Logical Architecture (How?): Develops abstract security blueprints and models showing how assets will be protected without specifying exact technologies. This includes security patterns, control strategies, and architectural designs.

Physical Architecture (With what?): Selects specific technologies, tools, and products that implement the logical architecture. This layer makes concrete decisions about security software, hardware, and infrastructure.

Component Architecture (Where?): Defines detailed configurations and deployment specifications for the selected technologies within the organization's environment.

Operational Architecture (Who?): Establishes governance, roles, responsibilities, and ongoing management procedures for maintaining the security architecture throughout its lifecycle.

Use Cases: SABSA is particularly effective for organizations seeking to demonstrate that security investments directly support business value, such as in public sector organizations, financial institutions, and enterprises requiring strong business-security alignment. It excels when organizations need to prove compliance by tracing every security control back to a specific business requirement or risk

docs.title: 2. TOGAF (The Open Group Architecture Framework)
docs.text:
TOGAF is an enterprise architecture framework that includes comprehensive security considerations through its Architecture Development Method (ADM), a phased approach to enterprise architecture development. TOGAF emphasizes security by design, embedding security requirements into every phase of architecture development rather than treating security as a post-implementation concern.

Use Cases: TOGAF is particularly valuable for large, complex enterprises requiring comprehensive, long-term enterprise architecture governance. Organizations implementing "Security by Design" initiatives use TOGAF to ensure security is considered from the architecture vision phase through implementation and operational phases. It is effective in organizations where business alignment and comprehensive IT governance are critical success factors.

docs.title: 3. Zachman Framework
docs.text:
The Zachman Framework is a widely used logical structure for organizing enterprise architecture artifacts. It is arranged as a matrix with six rows representing different stakeholder perspectives (Planner, Owner, Designer, Builder, etc) and six columns representing different aspects of the system (What, How, Where, Who, When, and Why).

Use Cases: The Zachman Framework is effective for organizations that need to systematically capture security requirements from multiple perspectives and demonstrate traceability of security controls back to original business requirements. It is valuable in regulated industries requiring evidence of security certification and compliance.

Other well know frameworks include COBIT, NIST CSF.

docs.title: 1. Scope
docs.text:
• Applies to AI systems placed on the EU market or used in the EU, regardless of origin.
  • Covers both public and private sector use.
  • Excludes personal/non‑professional use.

docs.title: 2. Key Definitions
docs.text:
• AI System - Software using ML, logic‑based, or statistical methods that generate outputs influencing environments.
  • Providers - Entities developing or placing AI systems on the market.
  • Deployers - Individuals or organizations deploying AI systems.

docs.title: 3. Risk Categories
docs.text:
The Act introduces a risk‑based framework:

1. Unacceptable Risk - Prohibited AI systems

  • Manipulation of human behaviour, opinions, and decisions

  • Classification of people based on their social behaviour

  • Real-time remote biometric identification (except for limited exceptions)

2. High Risk - Permitted subject to compliance with AI requirements

  • AI system applications listed in Annex III

  • AI systems in safety components already subject to a harmonized EU standard (Annex I)

3. Limited Risk - Permitted but subject to transparency obligations

Examples: chatbots, deepfakes (must disclose they’re AI).

4. Minimal Risk - Permitted without restrictions

Examples: spam filters, video games.

docs.title: 4. Prohibited AI systems
docs.text:
Use cases include:

  • Social scoring by governments

  • Manipulative AI exploiting vulnerabilities (children, disabled)

  • Biometric categorization based on sensitive attributes

  • Real‑time biometric identification in public spaces (exceptions for law enforcement)

  • Predictive policing based solely on profiling

  • Emotion recognition in workplaces and education

docs.title: 5. High‑Risk Applications
docs.text: High‑risk AI systems are those that impact safety or fundamental rights.

docs.title: Annex III (Applications)
docs.text:
Any application falling within Annex III categories that potentially threaten health, safety, fundamental rights, the environment, democracy, or the rule of law is automatically considered High risk.

  • Biometric identification & categorization

  • Critical infrastructure (transport, energy)

  • Education & vocational training

  • Employment & worker management

  • Access to essential services (credit scoring, social benefits)

  • Law enforcement

  • Migration, asylum & border control

  • Administration of justice & democratic processes

Obligations

  • Providers (developers/vendors) of high risk AI systems must carry out the conformity assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service

  • Deployers must conduct Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIA) before use

  • Effective from Q3 2026

docs.title: Annex I (Safety Components)
docs.text:
Annex I covers AI systems that are safety components of products already regulated under existing EU product safety laws.

  • Civil aviation, vehicles, marine equipment, medical devices, rail systems, personal protection, etc.,

  • These AI components must comply with the existing sectoral legislation (like the Medical Devices Regulation, Machinery Regulation, etc.).

  • Conformity assessment obligations for Annex I systems are aligned with those sectoral laws, not the standalone AI Act process - meaning they are enforceable once the AI Act enters into force (before August 2027) and the sectoral rules apply.

  • Oversight handled by an independent, accredited notified bodies

Conformity Assessment

Two pathways:

  • Internal Control (Self‑Assessment)

    • Applies to Annex III high risk applications (e.g., employment, essential services)

    • Providers may conduct self assessment if harmonized EU standards exist

    • If harmonized standards are missing, providers must follow common specifications (issued by the EU Commission)

    • Responsibility lies entirely with the provider to ensure compliance, maintain documentation, and issue a declaration of conformity

  • Third‑Party Assessment

    • Applies to Annex I systems (AI safety components in regulated products like aviation, medical devices, automotive)

    • Always required when harmonized standards are missing or incomplete

    • Also required for particularly sensitive high risk applications, such as biometric identification systems

    • Conducted by an independent, accredited notified body, ensuring impartiality and credibility.

Key compliance elements:

  • Risk management system

  • Data governance

  • Technical documentation

  • Logging & record‑keeping

  • Transparency to users

  • Human oversight

  • Accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity

Harmonized Standards

  • They are technical standards developed by European standardization bodies (like CEN, CENELEC, ETSI)

  • Provide technical guidance on how to comply with the essential requirements of EU legislation

  • Internal conformity assessment is sufficient when harmonized standards exist and the provider follows them

Example: Employment AI (recruitment tools)

  • An AI system screens CVs and ranks candidates

  • If harmonized standards exist for fairness and non discrimination in employment, the provider can self assess compliance by applying those standards

  • If no harmonized standard exists yet, the provider must undergo a third party assessment by a notified body to ensure impartial verification

Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA)

Steps:

  1. Define AI system & context

  2. Identify stakeholders & affected groups

  3. Assess impacts on fundamental rights (privacy, nondiscrimination, freedom of expression, access to justice)

  4. Evaluate severity & likelihood

  5. Document mitigation measures

  6. Establish oversight & accountability

  7. Ensure transparency & reporting

  8. Update regularly before deployment or when risks change

docs.title: 6. General Purpose AI (GPAI) Models
docs.text:
As models and systems are treated separately, a general-purpose AI model itself will not be classified as a high-risk AI system. However, High impact GPAI models (those with significant capabilities or risks) have stricter obligation requirements

  • Providers of GPAI models must document training data sources, evaluate systemic risks, and share technical information with downstream deployers.
  • High‑impact GPAI models must undergo risk assessments, adversarial testing, cybersecurity

Open‑source GPAI models are not considered high-risk, however they have to provide detailed summary about the content used for training and abide with EU copyright laws

docs.title: 7. Incident Reporting
docs.text:
• Serious incidents - Report within 15 days
  • Critical infrastructure disruption - Report immediately, within a maximum of 2 days

docs.title: 8. Sandbox Testing Facilities
docs.text:
• National authorities provide regulatory sandboxes
  • Controlled testing with regulator feedback
  • Especially useful for SMEs and startups

docs.title: 9. Enforcement & Penalties
docs.text:
• Supervised by national authorities and coordinated by the European AI Board
  • Penalties:
    • Up to €35M or 7% of global turnover for prohibited practices
    • Up to €15M or 3% of turnover for high‑risk/GPAI infringements
    • Up to €7.5M or 1% of turnover for misleading information

docs.title: 10. Implementation Timeline
docs.text:
• Aug 2024 - Act enters into force
  • Q1 2025 - Prohibited practices are enforceable
  • Q3 2025 - Obligations for GPAI models and governance structures (European AI Office, national authorities) are applicable.
  • Q3 2026 - High‑risk AI system requirements under Annex III (conformity assessments, FRIA, provider obligations) become fully enforceable.
  • Q3 2027 - Full enforcement of the Act

Exceptions:

  • High Risk AI Systems already on the market are not subject to the AI Act, if they were placed on the market before the Act entered into force

    Exception: If the system undergoes a significant change (e.g., retraining, new functionality, expanded scope), then it must comply with the Act

  • GPAI obligations start Aug 2026

  • Large‑scale EU IT systems in Freedom, Security & Justiec (e.g., Schengen), their compliance timeline is extended until 2030

docs.title: FedRAMP: Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program
docs.text:
FedRAMP standardizes security assessment, authorization, and continuous monitoring for cloud services used by U.S. federal agencies.

It leverages NIST SP 800-53 controls but adds cloud-specific requirements and enforces a “do once, use many times” authorization model via the JAB and agency P-ATO process.

Authorizations are scoped to Low, Moderate, or High impact levels, each with increasing control counts and stringency. Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) achieving FedRAMP authorization gain access to the federal marketplace and signal strong security posture to private-sector customers as well.

docs.title: 1. Purpose and Scope
docs.text: FedRAMP’s goal is to ensure that cloud services protecting federal data meet rigorous, baseline security requirements. It replaces redundant agency-by-agency assessments with a “do once, use many times” model so that CSPs can achieve a single authorization and have it reused across multiple federal agencies.

docs.title: 2. Governance and Oversight
docs.text:
• Managing Office: General Services Administration (GSA) Technology Transformation Services
  • Authorization Bodies:
    • Joint Authorization Board (JAB): Senior representatives from DoD, DHS, and GSA grant Provisional Authority to Operate (P-ATO)
    • Agency Authorization: Individual federal agencies grant an Authority to Operate (ATO) based on their own risk decisions
  • Community Working Groups: Industry and public contributors shape evolving guidance (FedRAMP 20X initiative)

docs.title: 3. Requirements Foundation
docs.text:
FedRAMP baselines its controls on NIST SP 800-53, tailoring them for cloud environments. There are three impact levels—Low, Moderate, and High—which correspond to the potential impact on federal operations and data confidentiality, integrity, and availability:

Impact Level Typical Data Sensitivity Control Baseline Size Low Public or non-sensitive ~125 controls Moderate Controlled Unclassified Information ~325 controls High National security or highly sensitive ~425 controls

Each baseline includes mandatory controls and control enhancements for continuous monitoring, incident response, encryption, identity management, and more.

docs.title: 4. Authorization Process
docs.text:
1. Preparation

    • Conduct a gap analysis against the FedRAMP baseline
    • Assemble the System Security Plan (SSP) and supporting documentation

  2. Assessment

    • Engage an accredited Third-Party Assessment Organization (3PAO)
    • Perform security testing and produce a Security Assessment Report (SAR)

  3. Authorization

    • Submit SSP and SAR to either the JAB (for P-ATO) or a sponsoring agency (for ATO)
    • The authorizing body reviews, issues an ATO or P-ATO, and publishes the package to the FedRAMP Marketplace

  4. Continuous Monitoring

    • CSPs perform monthly scans, annual assessments, and report findings via the FedRAMP Secure Repository
    • Ongoing change control and vulnerability management ensure sustained compliance

docs.title: 5. Benefits of FedRAMP Authorization
docs.text:
• Market Access: Mandatory for any CSP serving federal agencies; listed in the FedRAMP Marketplace
  • Efficiency: Eliminates duplicate security reviews across agencies
  • Credibility: Signals adherence to one of the world’s most rigorous cloud security programs
  • Scalability: One authorization can support multiple customers, including state/local governments and the private sector

docs.title: FedRAMP Marketplace
docs.text: The FedRAMP Marketplace is the official, publicly accessible directory that supports the U.S. government's secure cloud adoption efforts. Think of it as a centralized hub where federal agencies, CSPs, and 3PAOs converge to streamline and scale cloud security authorizations.

docs.title: What It Contains
docs.text:
• Cloud Service Offerings (CSOs) that have achieved a FedRAMP designation (e.g., Authorized, In Process)
  • Federal agencies that have sponsored or authorized a CSO
  • 3PAOs accredited to perform FedRAMP assessments

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text:
• Simplifies procurement: Agencies can reuse existing security authorizations instead of starting from scratch
  • Promotes transparency: Everyone can see which cloud products meet FedRAMP standards
  • Accelerates cloud adoption: Reduces redundant effort and speeds up secure cloud deployment across government
  • Supports “Do Once, Use Many”: A CSP’s FedRAMP package can be reused by multiple agencies, saving time and cost

Reference: FedRAMP Marketplace website

docs.title: FISMA (Federal Information Security Management Act), 2014
docs.text:
FISMA is a United States federal law that defines a comprehensive framework to protect government information, operations, and assets against natural and manmade threats.

Amended by FISMA 2014, the act requires each federal agency in the US government to develop, document, and implement an agency-wide information security program to protect sensitive data and information systems that support the operations and assets of the agency, including those provided or managed by another agency, third-party vendor, or service provider.

FISMA requires agency program officials, chief information officers (CIOs), and inspectors general (IGs) to implement information security policies and controls.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
FISMA itself tasks NIST (in consultation with OMB) to publish standards and guidelines—primarily the NIST SP 800-series—that agencies must follow. There isn’t a formal “FISMA Implementation Project” title; rather, NIST’s publications such as:

  • SP 800-53
  • SP 800-37
  • SP 800-60

serve as the de facto implementation resources.

Note: The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) plays a central oversight role in federal cybersecurity governance.

docs.title: Key Compliance requirements
docs.text:
While FISMA compliance defines a vast and detailed set of security requirements, the high-level requirements can be summarized as follows:

  • Maintain an inventory of federal information systems (including any cloud environments).
  • Categorize systems per FIPS 199 and NIST SP 800-60 (low, moderate, high impact).
  • Develop and update a System Security Plan (SSP) with associated Plan of Action & Milestones (POA&M).
  • Select and implement baseline controls from FIPS 200 and NIST SP 800-53.
  • Conduct risk assessments and adjust controls as needed.
  • Perform Security Assessment and Authorization under NIST SP 800-37 (formerly “certification and accreditation”).
  • Institute continuous monitoring to detect changes in security posture.

docs.title: Non-compliance
docs.text:
FISMA does not prescribe criminal fines or jail time, but non-compliance can trigger:

  • Withholding of OMB or agency funding
  • Formal findings by Inspectors General
  • Suspension or debarment of contractors
  • Negative audit reports and agency-level sanctions

These indirect “penalties” serve as powerful levers to enforce compliance rather than statutory fines.

docs.title: Generally Accepted Privacy Principles (GAPP)
docs.text:
Generally Accepted Privacy Principles (GAPP) is a comprehensive privacy framework developed jointly by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants (CICA).

It’s 10 principles guides organizations—especially accounting firms and service providers—in designing, implementing, and maintaining effective privacy programs that manage personal information ethically and in line with legal requirements. Mandatory for publicly traded U.S. companies.

Framework Structure - GAPP is built on a single overarching privacy objective. Personal information must be collected, used, retained, and disclosed in accordance with the commitments in the organization’s privacy notice and with criteria defined in the GAPP framework.

This objective is supported by 10 Privacy Principles:

  1. Management: Defining and assigning accountability for privacy policies.

  2. Notice & Communication: Informing individuals about privacy policies and the purposes of data collection.

  3. Choice and consent: Providing individuals with options regarding the collection, use, and disclosure of their data.

  4. Collection: Limiting data collection to only what is necessary.

  5. Use, retention and disposal: Limiting the use of data to the stated purposes, retaining it only as long as necessary, and then disposing of it securely.

  6. Access: Giving individuals access to their personal information for review and updates.

  7. Disclosure to third parties: Limiting disclosure to third parties and requiring individual consent.

  8. Security for privacy: Protecting personal information with appropriate security measures.

  9. Quality: Maintaining accurate, complete, and relevant personal information.

  10. Monitoring and enforcement: Monitoring compliance and having procedures to address complaints.

Implementation and Benefits

  • Privacy Program Design: Use GAPP’s objectives and criteria to build policies, procedures, and controls.

  • SOC 2 Integration: GAPP aligns directly with SOC 2’s Privacy Trust Services Criteria, enabling streamlined audits.

  • Global Compliance: Provides a solid foundation for meeting regulations like GDPR and CCPA.

  • Accountability & Transparency: Embeds roles and responsibilities, risk assessments, and ongoing monitoring into the privacy program.

docs.title: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), 2016
docs.text: The GDPR aims to protect the data of all EU residents and make it easier for organizations to understand and comply with data protection rules. Even if your organization does not have a location in the EU, if you handle the personal data of any EU citizen, you must comply or risk fines of up to 4% of annual revenue or €20 million (whichever is higher).

docs.title: Basic Terminology (Chapter 1 – Article 4)
docs.text:
• Data Subject: Any person residing in the EU whose data is collected, held, or processed.
  • Data Controller: Entity responsible for determining the purpose and lawful basis for processing personal data.
  • Data Processor: Processes personal data on behalf of the controller.
  • Processing: Any automated or manual operation on personal data (collection, storage, retrieval, etc.).
  • Personal Data: Any information that can identify a person directly or indirectly (e.g., name, email, photos, location data, online identifiers).

docs.title: Special Categories of Personal Data (Sensitive Data – Article 9)
docs.text:
• Race or ethnicity
  • Political opinion
  • Religious or philosophical beliefs
  • Genetic and biometric data
  • Health data
  • Sex life or sexual orientation

Processing is prohibited by default unless a specific legal basis applies (e.g., explicit consent, public health).

docs.title: Consent
docs.text:
Consent must be:

  • Freely given
  • Specific
  • Informed
  • Unambiguous

It can be provided via a statement or explicit affirmative action.

docs.title: Seven Principles of GDPR (Chapter 2 – Articles 5–10)
docs.text:
1. Lawfulness, fairness, transparency – Lawful basis for each activity, clear communication.
  2. Purpose limitation – Process only for specified purposes.
  3. Data minimization – Collect only what is necessary.
  4. Accuracy – Keep data accurate and up to date.
  5. Storage limitation – Retain data only as long as needed.
  6. Integrity & confidentiality (security) – Protect data with appropriate safeguards.
  7. Accountability – Demonstrate compliance with records and measures.

docs.title: Rights of Data Subjects (Chapter 3)
docs.text:
• Right to be informed (Art. 12–14): Know how personal data is collected and used.
  • Right of access (Art. 15): View and request copies of personal data.
  • Right to data portability (Art. 20): Transfer data to another controller in machine-readable format.
  • Right to withdraw consent (Art. 7): Withdraw previously given consent.
  • Right to rectification (Art. 16): Correct inaccurate or outdated data.
  • Right to erasure / be forgotten (Art. 17): Request deletion of personal data (subject to exemptions).
  • Right to restrict processing (Art. 18): Request suppression of data.
  • Right to object (Art. 21): Object to processing.
  • Right to object to automated processing (Art. 22): Challenge decisions made solely by automated means.

docs.title: Lawful Bases for Processing (Article 6)
docs.text: Lawful Basis When It Applies Example Consent Clear, specific, informed, freely given consent — Contract Necessary for contract performance or pre-contract steps Ecommerce site processing address for delivery Legal Obligation Required to comply with EU or Member State law Employer reporting salary data to tax authorities Vital Interests Protects vital interests of data subject or another person Hospital accessing patient history in emergency Public Task Task in public interest or official authority Government agency maintaining a public register Legitimate Interests Necessary for controller’s legitimate interests unless overridden by rights Bank fraud prevention

docs.title: Special Categories (Article 9 Exceptions)
docs.text:
Processing sensitive data requires both a lawful basis (Art. 6) and one of the exceptions in Art. 9(2), such as:

  • Explicit consent
  • Employment/social security obligations
  • Vital interests
  • Public health protection
  • Archiving/research with safeguards

docs.title: Data Controller
docs.text:
• Decide why and how personal data is processed
  • Select compliant processors
  • Maintain records of processing activities (RoPA)
  • Ensure data protection by design/default
  • Notify authorities and data subjects of breaches
  • Facilitate subject rights

docs.title: Data Processor
docs.text:
• Process only on documented instructions
  • Ensure confidentiality of personnel
  • Implement security measures
  • Assist controller with compliance duties
  • Delete/return data after service ends
  • Maintain RoPA
  • Notify controller of breaches

docs.title: Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs)
docs.text:
DPIA identifies and minimizes risks associated with the processing of personal data. It is a requirement under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) for certain high-risk processing activities.

Mandatory for high-risk processing (Art. 35), e.g.:

  • Automated profiling with significant effects
  • Large-scale processing of sensitive data
  • Systematic monitoring of public areas

docs.title: Key Elements of DPIA
docs.text:
1. Description of processing operations and purposes
  2. Assessment of necessity and proportionality
  3. Risk assessment for data subjects
  4. Measures to address risks and demonstrate compliance

If risks cannot be mitigated, consult the Data Protection Authority (DPA) before proceeding.

docs.title: Conducting DPIA
docs.text:
