• Secure management approval and form a cross-functional team including IT, legal, and privacy experts
  • Define scope by describing processing purposes, data types (e.g., sensitive health data), and involved parties
  • Map data flows, assess necessity and proportionality, then evaluate risks to individuals' rights like privacy breaches
  • Identify mitigation measures such as encryption or access controls, document findings, and obtain sign-off for implementation
  • Review periodically or before changes, ensuring ongoing compliance.

Developing Data Maps and Inventories

Data maps visualize flows; inventories catalogue assets for compliance.

  • Inventory all personal data: categories (e.g., names, emails), sources, storage locations, and retention periods
  • Map flows: entry points, processors (vendors), transfers, and deletion processes using tools like spreadsheets or automated software
  • Maintain dynamically: update quarterly, integrate with RoPA, and audit for accuracy to meet regulations like GDPR Article 30.
  • Use for risk spotting, vendor management, and breach response.

docs.title: Breach Notification Rule
docs.text:
Organizations must notify the relevant supervisory authority of a personal data breach within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. If notification cannot be made within that period, reasons for the delay must be provided. In certain cases, affected individuals must also be informed “without undue delay.”

Exceptions: Notification to individuals is not required if:

  • Data was encrypted or otherwise rendered unintelligible
  • Measures have been taken to eliminate the risk
  • Notification would involve disproportionate effort (in which case a public communication may suffice)

Penalties: Failure to notify within 72 hours can result in fines of up to €10 million or 2% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher).

docs.title: Records of Processing Activities (RoPA)
docs.text:
Under Article 30, RoPA is a mandatory GDPR record for controllers/processors with over 250 employees or handling sensitive data.

Key elements include:

  • Data categories
  • Processing purposes
  • Recipients and transfers
  • Retention periods
  • Security measures

RoPA ensures accountability, supports DPIAs, and demonstrates compliance during audits. It should be maintained centrally, reviewed annually, and shared with authorities upon request.

docs.title: Penalties (Chapter 8)
docs.text: Type of Violation Maximum Fine Examples Lower-tier (Art. 83(4)) Up to €10 million or 2% of global turnover Not keeping records, failing to notify breaches, inadequate protection Higher-tier (Art. 83(5)) Up to €20 million or 4% of global turnover Violating principles, infringing rights, unlawful international transfers

docs.title: Deletion & Retention
docs.text:
• Article 5(1)(e): Data must be deleted once the purpose is achieved.
  • Exceptions: If another law requires retention (e.g., tax, employment), GDPR allows retention but mandates restricted access and secure storage.

docs.title: De-identification Techniques
docs.text:
• Pseudonymization: Reversible masking of identifiers (still considered PII under GDPR).
  • Anonymization: Irreversible removal of identifiers (no longer PII).
  • Tokenization: Replacement of sensitive data with non-sensitive tokens (common in financial data).

docs.title: HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act), 1996
What HIPAA Protects
docs.text: • Protected Health Information (PHI): Individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by covered entities/business associates, including electronic, paper, and oral forms.

docs.title: Who Must Comply
docs.text:
• Covered entities: Health plans, health care clearinghouses, and health care providers that conduct standard electronic transactions
  • Business associates: Vendors and service providers that create, receive, maintain, or transmit PHI on behalf of covered entities

docs.title: Key Titles
docs.text:
• Title I — Health Insurance Portability: Protects health insurance coverage for workers and families when they change or lose jobs
  • Title II — Administrative Simplification: Requires national standards for electronic health care transactions and identifiers, forming the basis for privacy and security rules for PHI

docs.title: Core Rules Under Title II
docs.text:
• Privacy Rule: Governs permissible uses and disclosures of PHI by covered entities, giving individuals rights over their health information
  • Security Rule: Requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to protect electronic PHI (ePHI)
  • Breach Notification Rule:
    • Mandates notifications to affected individuals (and regulators/media in some cases) after certain PHI breaches
    • Affected individuals must receive notice no later than 60 days after breach discovery, via first-class mail or email (if agreed), in plain language detailing the incident, exposed data, response actions, prevention steps, and contact info
    • For breaches impacting 500+ individuals, notify HHS (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services) and prominent local media within the same 60 days; smaller breaches go to HHS annually by year's end
  • Enforcement Rule: Establishes investigations, penalties, and procedures for non-compliance

Violations can lead to: - Civil penalties (fines up to millions of dollars) - Criminal charges in severe cases - Reputational damage

docs.title: Why It Matters
docs.text: HIPAA overrides state laws unless those laws offer greater privacy protections.

docs.title: CCPA vs HIPAA
docs.text:
• HIPAA: Governs PHI handled by covered entities (like hospitals, insurers) and their business associates
  • CCPA: Governs personal information of California residents handled by for-profit businesses, regardless of industry — unless exemptions apply

docs.title: HITECH (Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act), 2009
docs.text: The HITECH Act is a U.S. federal law enacted in 2009 as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA). It was designed to accelerate the adoption of electronic health records (EHRs) and strengthen the privacy and security protections under HIPAA.

docs.title: Purpose of HITECH
docs.text:
• Promote the widespread use of health information technology (HIT)
  • Improve quality, safety, and efficiency in healthcare delivery
  • Expand privacy and security protections for electronic health information
  • Provide financial incentives to healthcare providers for adopting certified EHR systems
  • Establish penalties for non-compliance with HIPAA privacy and security rules

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text: Feature Description Meaningful Use Incentives Providers who demonstrate “meaningful use” of certified EHRs receive Medicare/Medicaid incentive payments Stronger HIPAA Enforcement Increased penalties for data breaches and non-compliance; expanded enforcement authority Breach Notification Rule Requires covered entities and business associates to notify individuals and regulators of certain data breaches Extension to Business Associates Business associates (e.g., IT vendors, billing services) are directly subject to HIPAA security and breach notification rules Patient Empowerment Patients gain rights to access their electronic health records and request corrections ONC Codification Formalized the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) to lead national HIT strategy

docs.title: Why HITECH Was Enacted Despite HIPAA
docs.text: While HIPAA (1996) laid the foundation for protecting health information, it was written before electronic health records (EHRs) became widespread. By the late 2000s, the healthcare industry was rapidly digitizing, and HIPAA’s enforcement mechanisms and incentives weren’t keeping pace.

docs.title: 1. Modernize HIPAA for the Digital Age
docs.text:
• HIPAA didn’t fully address electronic data transmission, cloud storage, or digital breach risks
  • HITECH updated HIPAA’s Privacy and Security Rules to reflect the realities of EHRs and digital workflows

docs.title: 2. Strengthen Enforcement
docs.text:
• Before HITECH, HIPAA violations often resulted in minimal fines (e.g., $100 per violation)
  • HITECH introduced tiered penalties up to $1.5 million per violation category per year
  • Gave the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) more resources to investigate and enforce HIPAA violations

docs.title: 3. Extend HIPAA Liability to Business Associates
docs.text:
• HIPAA originally held covered entities accountable, but business associates weren’t directly liable
  • HITECH made business associates legally responsible for complying with HIPAA’s Security and Breach Notification Rules

docs.title: 4. Mandate Breach Notification
docs.text:
• HIPAA lacked a clear breach notification requirement
  • HITECH introduced the Breach Notification Rule, requiring covered entities and business associates to notify affected individuals and regulators when unsecured PHI is compromised

docs.title: 5. Incentivize EHR Adoption
docs.text: • HITECH launched the Meaningful Use program, offering financial incentives to providers who adopted certified EHR systems and used them to improve care

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Law Focus Why HITECH Was Needed HIPAA Privacy & security of health data Strong foundation, but outdated for digital health systems HITECH EHR adoption + HIPAA enforcement Modernized HIPAA, added breach rules, extended liability, and funded digital transformation

docs.title: HITRUST (Health Information Trust Alliance)
docs.text:
Created by Common Security Framework (CSF), it is a certifiable compliance and risk management framework. It is primarily used in the healthcare industry but has expanded into finance, technology, and other sectors that handle sensitive data.

What is the HITRUST Compliance Framework?

  • HITRUST CSF is a comprehensive, certifiable security and privacy framework.

  • It was designed to help organizations manage risk, comply with regulations, and demonstrate strong data protection practices.

  • The framework integrates and harmonizes multiple standards, including:

    • HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act).

    • HITECH Act (Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act).

    • ISO/IEC 27001 (international information security standard).

    • NIST Cybersecurity Framework.

    • PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard).

By combining these, HITRUST CSF reduces the complexity of meeting multiple compliance requirements.

Where is HITRUST Used?

  • Healthcare

Hospitals, insurance providers, and health tech companies use HITRUST to prove compliance with HIPAA and protect patient data.

Example: Electronic Health Record (EHR) vendors often pursue HITRUST certification to reassure clients.

  • Cloud & Technology Providers

Microsoft Azure, Office 365, and Dynamics 365 are HITRUST-certified, showing its adoption in cloud services.

Tech companies use it to demonstrate secure handling of sensitive customer data.

  • Financial Services

Banks and payment processors adopt HITRUST to align with PCI DSS and safeguard financial data.

  • Third-Party Vendors

Organizations require their business associates and partners to be HITRUST certified, ensuring a consistent security baseline across the supply chain.

Why Organizations Choose HITRUST

  • Streamlined compliance: Instead of juggling multiple audits, HITRUST provides a single, certifiable framework.

  • Trust & assurance: Certification signals to clients and regulators that the organization meets rigorous security standards.

  • Proven effectiveness: HITRUST reports that 99.4% of certified environments had no breaches in recent years.

docs.title: Incident reporting timeline under different Indian Institutions
Incident Reporting Timelines
docs.text: Institution Required Timeline Scope / What to Report CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team) 6 hours Report cybersecurity incidents (as defined in CERT-In Directions) to enable national incident response and coordination. DPDP Act / Data Protection Board 72 hours Notify the Data Protection Board and affected individuals of personal data breaches within 72 hours of becoming aware, per the DPDP Rules and operational guidance. NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) 24 hours (initial report) Member banks/participants must report security incidents affecting NPCI services or payment systems — initial reporting typically required within 24 hours, with follow-ups as per NPCI guidelines.

docs.title: Timeline conflict
docs.text:
• The rules come from different legal/regulatory regimes with distinct objectives: CERT-In focuses on national cybersecurity coordination and rapid technical response; the DPDP Act focuses on personal data protection and rights of affected individuals; NPCI focuses on payment-system integrity and financial sector risk management.
  • That creates overlapping obligations for the same incident: a breach affecting payment data may trigger CERT-In (6h), NPCI (24h), and DPDP (72h) reports — each with different addressees, formats, and follow-up requirements.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
• Treat the shortest applicable deadline as the operational trigger for initial reporting and triage (i.e., act within 6 hours to satisfy CERT-In), then prepare the sector-specific and data-privacy reports required at 24h and 72h with the specific content each regulator demands.

    Keep clear processes that map incident types to which regulations apply, who must be notified, and the evidence/content each regulator expects.

docs.title: Data & Log Retention
docs.text: Regulator Log Retention Data Retention Note CERT-In 180 days Subscriber info 5 years Applies to VPNs, cloud, hosting, intermediaries DPDP Act & Rules 2025 ≥1 year 3 years (special classes)7 years (consent managers) Notification to Data Principals before deletion RBI Supervisory access 5 years (KYC/AML), localized storage Directive 2018 mandates India-only storage

docs.title: ISO/IEC 27001-2022 & 27002 - Information Security Management System (ISMS)
docs.text:
• ISO/IEC 27001 specifies the requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an ISMS. Organizations can become formally certified to demonstrate a structured, risk-based approach to protecting confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information.

  • ISO/IEC 27002 complements 27001 by providing detailed best-practice guidance on selecting and implementing 93 security controls across organizational, people, physical, and technological domains. Unlike 27001 (which is certifiable), 27002 is not a management standard but a practical controls catalogue for risk treatment. It plays a supporting role to ISO/IEC 27001.

The clauses form the backbone of ISO 27001 compliance. Clauses 4–10 are mandatory requirements for certification, while Clauses 1–3 provide foundational context.

docs.title: Changes in Annexure Controls from ISO/IEC 27001:2013
docs.text:
• The control sets are now organized into four (4) categories or themes as opposed to fourteen (14) control domains. The 4 categories include Organizational, People, Physical, and Technological.

  • The total control count has been reduced—there are 21 less controls in the 2022 version; leading to a total of 93 controls.

  • There was a concentrated effort to avoid control redundancy. 24 controls in the 2022 version included merged controls from the 2013 version.

  • There are now 11 new controls to update the standard to the current information security and cyber security landscape.

  • Objectives for controls have been removed from ISO/IEC 27001:2022 standards.

docs.title: The 11 new control topics:
docs.text:
• Organizational Control:

    5.7. Threat intelligence

    5.23. Information security for use of cloud services

    5.30. ICT readiness for business continuity [ICT -Information & Communication Technology]

  • Physical Control:

    7.4. Physical security monitoring

  • Technological Control:

    8.9. Configuration management

    8.10. Information deletion

    8.11. Data masking

    8.12. Data leakage prevention

    8.16. Monitoring activities

    8.23. Web filtering

    8.28. Secure coding

docs.title: 1. High-Level Comparison
docs.text: Aspect SOC 2 ISO 27001 Type Attestation report (Type I/Type II) Certifiable management system standard Governing Body AICPA (AT 101 → SSAE 18 attestation standards) ISO/IEC (International Organization for Standardization) Scope Controls relevant to the Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy) Information Security Management System (ISMS) covering any risk to information assets Criteria vs Requirements Must meet chosen Trust Services Criteria (flexible selection beyond Security) Must satisfy all clauses 4–10 and Annex A controls Certification/Attestation CPA issues an attestation opinion—no formal “certificate” Accredited body issues certificate of compliance Geographical Reach Primarily U.S., recognized by U.S. customers Global, often required by international partners Report Audience Customers, prospects, business partners (restricted use) Regulators, customers, internal/external auditors Report Detail Level Type I: control design at a point in timeType II: design + operating effectiveness over a period Ongoing: risk assessments, internal audits, management reviews; certificate renewed every 3 years with annual surveillance audits Renewal Cycle Type I one-off; Type II annually (or per engagement) Re-certification every 3 years; surveillance audits annually

docs.title: 2. Similarities
docs.text:
• Both frameworks emphasize a risk-based approach and continuous improvement.
  • Each demands independent validation by qualified auditors (CPAs for SOC 2, accredited bodies for ISO 27001).
  • Core security domains overlap: access control, change management, incident response, physical security, vendor management.
  • Both can serve as building blocks for broader compliance (e.g., HIPAA, GDPR, ISO 27701).

docs.title: 1. Flexibility vs. Completeness
docs.text:
• SOC 2: Lets you choose which Trust Services Criteria to include beyond the mandatory Security principle.
  • ISO 27001: Requires all 93 Annex A controls (unless scoped out in your SoA) and full ISMS lifecycle.

docs.title: 2. Certification vs. Attestation
docs.text:
• ISO 27001: Yields a certificate you can display and publicize.
  • SOC 2: Provides an auditor’s report with detailed results—typically shared under NDA.

docs.title: 3. Global Recognition
docs.text:
• ISO 27001: De facto international standard, often a prerequisite in Europe, Asia, and large enterprise procurement.
  • SOC 2: Significant weight in North America, especially for SaaS/cloud service vendors.

docs.title: 4. Process Orientation
docs.text:
• ISO 27001: Mandates establishing, implementing, operating, monitoring, reviewing, and improving an ISMS (Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle).
  • SOC 2: Focuses on testing controls against predefined criteria during an audit period.

docs.title: ISO 27001
docs.text:
• You need an internationally recognized certification.
  • You require a holistic ISMS integrating policies, risk assessments, internal audits, and management reviews.
  • Your customers or regulators explicitly require ISO 27001.

docs.title: SOC 2
docs.text:
• Your primary market is U.S.-based customers demanding detailed security/privacy attestation.
  • You want flexibility in selecting only the Trust Services Criteria that matter to your service.
  • You prefer a detailed, auditor-tested report over a high-level certificate.

docs.title: Both
docs.text:
• You serve a global customer base plus U.S. enterprises.
  • You’re building a mature security program and want to leverage one audit framework to support multiple compliance requirements.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
• It is a stand‑alone standard for business continuity.
  • Follows the Annex SL High Level Structure (HLS) — the same management system framework used in ISO 27001:2013 and ISO 27001:2022.
  • Because the HLS is consistent, ISO 22301:2019 can integrate smoothly with either version of ISO 27001 (2013 & 2022) without modification.
  • There is no dependency on which ISO 27001 version you use — integration aligns clauses 4–10 (context, leadership, planning, etc.), not Annex A controls.
  • Clause 8 diverges between ISO 27001 and ISO 22301.

docs.title: Normative Reference
docs.text:
• ISO 22300 series (Security and resilience).
  • Unlike ISO/IEC 27001, which has a detailed Annex A list of security controls, ISO 22301:2019 does not include an “Annex A” control catalogue.

docs.title: Why ISO 22301 ?
docs.text:
• ISO 22301 is a management system requirements standard — it specifies what your BCMS must achieve, not a prescriptive list of controls.
  • Clauses (4 through 10) set requirements for context, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, and improvement.
  • The standard expects organizations to identify their own continuity strategies, solutions, and procedures based on Business Impact Analysis (BIA) and risk assessment.

docs.title: Divergence in Clause 8 (Operation)
docs.text:
• ISO 27001 Clause 8: Focuses on information security risk treatment and implementing controls from Annex A.
  • ISO 22301 Clause 8: Focuses on business continuity planning, including BIA, continuity strategies, and recovery procedures.

docs.title: 1. Business Impact Analysis (BIA) – Clause 8.2.2
docs.text:
• Identifies critical activities, dependencies, and the impact of disruptions.
  • Helps define Recovery Time Objectives (RTOs) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPOs).

docs.title: 2. Continuity Risk Assessment – Clause 8.2.3
docs.text:
• Focuses on risks that could disrupt operations — not just information assets.
  • Includes natural disasters, supply chain failures, pandemics, etc.

docs.title: 3. Business Continuity Strategies – Clause 8.3
docs.text:
• Defines how the organization will maintain or restore operations during a disruption.
  • Includes alternate sites, manual workarounds, and resource reallocation.

docs.title: 4. Business Continuity Plans and Procedures – Clause 8.4
docs.text:
• Documents step‑by‑step actions for responding to incidents.
  • Includes communication plans, escalation paths, and recovery workflows.

docs.title: 5. Exercise and Testing – Clause 8.5
docs.text:
• Requires regular testing of continuity plans through simulations, drills, or tabletop exercises.
  • Validates readiness and identifies gaps.

docs.title: 6. Evaluation of Business Continuity Capability – Clause 8.6
docs.text:
• Reviews effectiveness of continuity arrangements post‑exercise or post‑incident.
  • Drives continual improvement.

docs.title: 7. Recovery Objectives
docs.text: • Explicit definition of RTOs and RPOs for critical processes — not required in ISO 27001.

docs.title: 8. Incident Response Integration
docs.text:
• ISO 27001 includes incident response for security events.
  • ISO 22301 expands this to all types of disruptions — operational, environmental, and human factors.

Read our article about BCMS and BIA

docs.title: ISO/IEC 27005 - information Security Risk Management
docs.text:
It supports organizations in implementing ISO/IEC 27001 by detailing how to identify, assess, evaluate, and treat information security risks. The latest edition is ISO/IEC 27005:2022, published in October 2022.

ISO 27005 is a guidance standard; Not certifiable.

docs.title: Why ISO/IEC 27005 Matters
docs.text:
• Helps organizations systematically manage risks instead of ad‑hoc control selection.
  • Provides a structured methodology for risk assessment and treatment.
  • Ensures alignment with ISO/IEC 27001, making certification efforts more effective.
  • Widely recognized as a best practice framework for risk management in information security.

Also, checkout the articles IT Risk concepts and IT Risk Management process

docs.title: ISO 27005 vs ISO 31000
docs.text:
• Purpose: Provides principles and guidelines for enterprise‑wide risk management.
  • Scope: Covers all organizational risks — strategic, financial, operational, environmental, safety, and information security.
  • Audience: Any organization seeking a structured approach to risk management.
  • Certification: Not certifiable; it is a guidance framework.
  • Latest Edition: ISO 31000:2018.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The NIST CSF 2.0 is a voluntary, risk-based framework designed by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology to help organizations of any size manage and reduce cybersecurity risk.

Core to CSF 2.0 are six functions that form a continuous improvement lifecycle:

  • Govern: Establish governance policies, roles, and oversight (new in 2.0).

  • Identify: Inventory assets, understand business context, and assess risk.

  • Protect: Implement safeguards such as access control, training, and data security.

  • Detect: Continuously monitor for anomalies and cybersecurity events.

  • Respond: Plan and execute actions to contain and mitigate incidents.

  • Recover: Restore systems and services while incorporating lessons learned.

Implementation Tiers: These describe the maturity of an organization's cybersecurity risk management, ranging from Partial (Tier 1) to Adaptive (Tier 4), indicating a progression from less formal to more proactive approaches.

docs.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5.1.1 controls
docs.text:
The most comprehensive and standardized catalog of security and privacy controls (it defines controls – not just policies) used across U.S. federal agencies, critical infrastructure, and increasingly by private enterprises for robust cybersecurity governance.

Full name: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations

What Are NIST SP 800-53 Controls?

  • Developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST).

  • Provides a catalog of 400+ controls for securing information systems and protecting privacy.

  • Used to implement FISMA, FedRAMP, and align with NIST CSF, ISO 27001, and other frameworks.

  • Controls are grouped into 20 families, each addressing a specific security domain.

docs.title: PCI-DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
Introduction
docs.text:
The PCI Data Security Standard v4.0 (published March 31, 2022) is an information security standard for businesses that handle payment card (both credit and debit) information. It was created by the PCI Security Standards Council that includes every major payment card company - Visa, MasterCard, Discover, American Express, JCB and UnionPay.

These businesses are expected to comply with PCI DSS, enforced through assessments via Self-Assessment Questionnaires (SQA) or Qualified Security Assessors (QSAs) and they can be fined or penalized if they don't.

The standard’s 12 requirements fall under six objectives:

  1. Build and maintain a secure network

    • Install and maintain network security controls
    • Apply secure configurations to all system components

  2. Protect cardholder data

    • Protect stored account data
    • Protect cardholder data with strong cryptography during transmission

  3. Maintain a vulnerability management program

    • Protect all systems and networks from malicious software
    • Develop and maintain secure systems and software

  4. Implement strong access controls

    • Restrict access to system components and account data by business need-to-know
    • Identify users and authenticate access to system components
    • Restrict physical access to cardholder

  5. Regularly monitor and test networks

    • Log and monitor all access to system components and cardholder data
    • Test security of systems and networks regularly

  6. Maintain an information security policy

    • Support information security with organizational policies and programs

docs.title: Merchant Level
docs.text:
Annual transaction volume determines your merchant level (Level 1–4).

Merchant Level

  • Level 1 - More than 6 million

  • Level 2 - 1 to 6 million

  • Level 3 - 20,000 to 1 million

  • Level 4 - Fewer than 20,000

PCI DSS compliance assessment is fundamentally an annual requirement, but it includes mandatory quarterly components.

  • Annually (Annual Assessment/Attestation): All entities (merchants and service providers) must validate their compliance with PCI DSS requirements once a year.

    • Level 1 Merchants/Service Providers: Require a formal Report on Compliance (ROC) performed by a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA).

    • Level 2-4 Merchants: Generally, require a self-validated Self-Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ) and an Attestation of Compliance (AOC).

    • Payment environment determines which SAQ type applies depending on how a merchant accepts and processes cardholder data (e.g., e commerce, in store terminals, outsourcing, storage of card data, etc.).

  • Quarterly (Network Scans): If you have external-facing IP addresses, you must conduct quarterly vulnerability scans performed by a PCI-approved scanning vendor (ASV).

  • Annual Penetration Testing: In addition to the annual assessment, a penetration test of the network and applications is required at least annually.

Key Takeaway: While you submit your formal compliance validation once a year, you must perform quarterly vulnerability scans to maintain that compliance throughout the year.

docs.title: Self Assessment Questionnaire (SAQ)
docs.text:
• It’s a validation tool created by the PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC).

  • Merchants and service providers use it to self evaluate their compliance with the PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard).

  • Instead of always undergoing a full external audit, smaller or lower risk entities can complete the SAQ to demonstrate they meet PCI DSS requirements.

What are SAQs for?

  • Compliance Reporting: They allow merchants/service providers to report their PCI DSS compliance status to their acquiring bank or payment brands.

  • Risk Reduction: By answering the SAQ, organizations confirm they have the required security controls in place to protect cardholder data.

  • Scoping Tool: Different SAQ types apply depending on how you handle cardholder data (e.g., e commerce only, in store terminals, fully outsourced processing).

  • Alternative to Full Audit: For smaller merchants (PCI Level 2 - 4), SAQs replace the need for a full Report on Compliance (RoC) by a Qualified Security Assessor.

How They Work

  • Each SAQ is a set of yes/no questions aligned to PCI DSS requirements.

  • At the end, the merchant signs an Attestation of Compliance (AoC) confirming they meet the requirements.

  • The completed SAQ is submitted to the acquiring bank or card brand as proof of compliance.

docs.title: Cardholder Data Environment
docs.text:
PCI DSS system categorization and scoping involve identifying the Cardholder Data Environment (CDE) and connected systems to determine applicable controls and SAQ type.

The CDE includes people, processes, and technology handling cardholder data (CHD) or Sensitive Authentication Data (SAD), plus connected systems. Start by inventorying all CHD/SAD flows, storage locations, and processing points using data discovery tools or diagrams. Connected systems (e.g., those sharing networks) must be scoped if they impact CDE security.

Categorize Systems

  • In-Scope (CDE Core): Systems directly storing, processing, or transmitting CHD/SAD.

  • Connected-to-CDE: Systems on the same network or with logical access to CDE; apply segmentation (e.g., firewalls) to limit scope.

  • Out-of-Scope: Isolated systems with no CDE connectivity; verify annually via testing.

Scoping Steps

  1. Map data flow diagrams showing CHD entry, movement, and exit points.

  2. Segment networks to isolate CDE (Requirement 1).

  3. Select SAQ based on payment methods (e.g., SAQ A for fully outsourced CNP, SAQ D for others)

  4. Document scope in a report with diagrams and justifications

docs.title: Storing CHD & SAD
docs.text:
1. Cardholder Data (CHD)

Cardholder data can be stored by merchants if there is a legitimate business need and it is protected (typically via encryption). It includes:

  • Primary Account Number (PAN): The unique 15- or 16-digit credit or debit card number.

  • Cardholder Name: The name of the individual to whom the card was issued.

  • Expiration Date: The month and year the card expires.

  • Service Code: A three- or four-digit number in the magnetic stripe that specifies acceptance requirements and limitations for the card.

The full PAN must be rendered unreadable if stored, using methods like encryption, truncation, or hashing. Name, expiration date, and service code are included only when linked with the full PAN.

2. Sensitive Authentication Data (SAD)

SAD is highly sensitive information used to authorize transactions. According to PCI DSS version 4.0, SAD must never be stored after authorization, even if it is encrypted (except for issuers with justified needs under strict controls like strong cryptography). It includes:

  • Full Track Data: The complete data contained on the card's magnetic stripe or equivalent data on a chip.

  • Card Verification Codes: Also known as CVV2, CVC2, CID, or CAV2, these are the 3- or 4-digit security codes printed on the front or back of the card.

  • PINs and PIN Blocks: Personal Identification Numbers and the encrypted blocks of data used to transport them during a transaction.

docs.title: Tokenization
docs.text:
A data protection technique used in payment security.

  • It replaces sensitive cardholder data (like the Primary Account Number, PAN) with a random, unique “token”.

  • It is primarily used to secure transactions. By storing a token instead of a credit card number, a merchant reduces their "attack surface." If their database is breached, the tokens are worthless to hackers without access to the separate "token vault".

  • The token has no exploitable value if intercepted — it cannot be mathematically reversed to reveal the original card number.

  • The real card data is stored securely in a token vault (usually managed by a PCI DSS compliant provider) which is the only place the token can be mapped back to the original data.

  • Merchants and systems then use the token instead of the actual card number for transactions, recurring billing, or analytics.

Benefits of Tokenization

  • Reduces PCI DSS scope (fewer systems handle real card data).

  • Enhances security — tokens are useless to attackers.

  • Supports business processes like recurring payments without storing PANs.

  • Simplifies compliance and lowers audit costs.

docs.title: Types of SAQ forms
docs.text:
There are 9 Self Assessment Questionnaires (SAQs) under PCI DSS. They are designed for different merchant environments depending on how you accept and process cardholder data:

  • SAQ A applies to card-not-present (CNP) merchants, including e-commerce and mail/telephone order (MOTO), who fully outsource all payment processing to a PCI DSS-compliant third-party service provider. These merchants do not electronically store, process, or transmit cardholder data on their systems.

  • SAQ A-EP targets e-commerce merchants who outsource payment processing but maintain websites or elements (like payment forms) that could impact transaction security. Unlike SAQ A, these merchants have partial control over the payment page, though they still avoid direct electronic handling of cardholder data.

  • SAQ B applies to merchants processing cardholder data only via imprint machines or standalone, non-networked dial-out terminals, with no electronic transmission or storage of card data. It covers a limited set of PCI DSS requirements like physical access controls, policies, and restricting data access.

    Standalone dial-out terminals are independent payment devices, typically countertop credit card readers, that connect directly to a payment processor via a standard analogue phone line (dial-up) rather than the internet or a network. They process transactions offline by dialling out to authorize cards, ensuring no cardholder data enters your internal systems.

  • SAQ B-IP targets merchants using standalone, PTS-approved point-of-interaction (POI) devices connected via IP (modern, standalone payment terminals) to process card data, but with no electronic storage or other non-terminal functions handling cardholder data. It includes more comprehensive requirements than SAQ B, such as network security and vulnerability management for the IP-connected devices.

  • SAQ C applies to merchants and service providers using payment application systems connected to the internet or other public networks, where they process, store, or transmit cardholder data electronically. It covers most PCI DSS requirements, including firewalls, access controls, encryption, and monitoring, but excludes those fully addressed by validated payment applications.

    Payment application systems are comprehensive software platforms (often installed on merchant servers or devices) that handle full payment processing workflows, including card reading, authorization, settlement, and reporting—requiring broader PCI DSS scoping and PA-DSS validation.

    Virtual terminal (VT) solutions, by contrast, are lightweight web-based interfaces hosted by payment providers where merchants manually key in card details for card-not-present (CNP) transactions like phone orders, minimizing merchant PCI burden to SAQ A or A-EP.

  • SAQ C-VT is for merchants using only virtual terminal (VT) solutions provided by a PCI DSS-validated payment processor, where no electronic cardholder data storage occurs on merchant systems. It focuses on a subset of requirements like secure authentication, physical security, and transmission encryption, with fewer questions (around 79) than full SAQ C.

    Virtual terminal (VT) solutions are web-based or software payment interfaces that let merchants manually enter customer card details (via phone, email, or in-person) to process transactions without physical hardware. They appear as secure browser dashboards or apps on any internet-connected device like a laptop, tablet, or phone.

  • SAQ P2PE-HW SAQ applies for merchants using only hardware payment terminals in a validated Point-to-Point Encryption (P2PE) solution listed by the PCI Security Standards Council (PCI SSC). Merchants qualify if all payment processing occurs via approved PCI P2PE hardware terminals, with no clear-text cardholder data accessible on any computer systems or electronic media outside these devices. The P2PE solution must encrypt data from capture to decryption, and no sensitive data is stored post-authorization.

    They encrypt card data instantly upon card read (chip, swipe, or tap), transmitting it in ciphertext directly to a decryption gateway without exposing cleartext PAN in the merchant environment—qualifying for reduced PCI SAQ P2PE-HW scope.

  • SAQ D is the most comprehensive PCI DSS Self-Assessment Questionnaire, applicable separately to merchants and service providers that do not qualify for any other SAQ type.

    SAQ D covers all 12 PCI DSS requirements for entities that store, process, or transmit cardholder data using complex systems not fitting simpler SAQs, such as those with custom payment applications, internet-connected POS, or multi-tenant service providers. It serves as the default "catch-all" for ineligible cases like SAQ A through C-VT.

    Full scope (329 Questions) includes network security (firewalls, segmentation), data protection (encryption, masking), vulnerability management, access controls, monitoring, and policy maintenance.Involves detailed testing procedures, such as reviewing configurations, interviewing personnel, and examining logs across all system components.

SAQ form summary

Payment Setup Recommended SAQ Fully outsourced CNP (no merchant page) SAQ A E-commerce with partial control SAQ A-EP Standalone dial-out terminals SAQ B IP-connected POI devices SAQ B-IP Internet-connected apps SAQ C Virtual terminals only SAQ C-VT Hardware payment terminals in a P2PE solution SAQ P2PE HW All others/complex SAQ D

docs.title: Non-Compliance
docs.text:
Failing to comply with PCI DSS can lead to severe financial penalties, reputational damage, increased risk of data breaches, and even loss of the ability to process credit card payments.

Financial Penalties

  • Fines from payment brands (Visa, Mastercard, etc.) can range from $5,000 to $100,000 per month depending on the severity and duration of non-compliance.

  • Increased transaction fees may be imposed by acquiring banks as a risk premium.

  • Liability for fraud losses if a breach occurs due to non-compliance.

Security Risks

  • Higher vulnerability to data breaches, exposing cardholder data and leading to massive cleanup costs.

  • Legal liabilities from affected customers or partners, especially under data protection laws like GDPR or CCPA.

Business Disruption

  • Loss of card processing privileges — banks or payment processors may revoke your ability to accept credit cards.

  • Operational downtime during investigations and remediation efforts.

Reputational Damage

  • Loss of customer trust due to perceived negligence in protecting sensitive data.

  • Negative media coverage and long-term brand impact.

Compliance Fallout

  • Audits and investigations triggered by non-compliance or breach.

  • Mandatory remediation plans and stricter oversight from payment processors.

docs.title: RACI Matrix
docs.text:
A RACI matrix (also called a RACI chart) is a responsibility assignment matrix used in project management.

  • R – Responsible: The person(s) who do the work.
  • A – Accountable: The one ultimately answerable for the task’s success.
  • C – Consulted: People whose input is needed before decisions or actions.
  • I – Informed: People who need updates but are not directly involved.

Why RACI matrix ?

  • Clarity of roles: Prevents overlap or gaps in responsibility.
  • Improved accountability: Ensures every task has a clear owner.
  • Better communication: Identifies who needs to be consulted or informed.
  • Efficiency: Reduces delays caused by unclear decision-making.
  • Conflict reduction: Minimizes disputes over “who should do what.”

How to use it ?

  1. List tasks/deliverables: Break down the project into specific activities.
  2. Identify roles: List all team members or stakeholder groups.
  3. Assign RACI categories: For each task, mark who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed.
  4. Validate assignments: Ensure each task has exactly one Accountable person and at least one Responsible person.
  5. Communicate and share: Make the matrix visible to the team to avoid confusion.
  6. Review regularly: Update the matrix as the project evolves.

⚠️ Key Considerations

  • Avoid too many “C” roles: Over-consulting slows progress.
  • Ensure one “A” per task: Multiple Accountables cause confusion.
  • Balance workload: Don’t overload one person with too many “R” roles.
  • Not a governance model: RACI clarifies responsibilities but doesn’t replace policies or organizational charts.

docs.title: RBI IT Governance Directions, 2023
docs.text:
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued a comprehensive regulation titled “Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices Directions, 2023”, These directions apply to: Scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, payment banks, credit bureaus, Financial Institutions.

Structured breakdown of the key mandates:

docs.title: IT Governance Framework
docs.text:
• Board Oversight Establish an IT Strategy Committee and ensure IT governance is aligned with business goals.
  • Senior Management Role Must implement and monitor IT policies and controls.
  • IT Steering Committee Required to oversee IT projects and performance.

docs.title: IT Infrastructure & Services Management
docs.text:
• Third-Party Arrangements Must be governed by robust contracts and risk assessments.
  • Change & Patch Management Formalized procedures for updates and fixes.
  • Audit Trails & Logging Mandatory for all critical applications to ensure traceability.
  • Cryptographic Controls Strong encryption standards for data transmission and storage.

docs.title: IT & Information Security Risk Management
docs.text:
• Cybersecurity Policy Must be documented and reviewed annually.
  • Vulnerability Assessment & Penetration Testing Required periodically.
  • Incident Response Entities must analyze cyber incidents and implement corrective/preventive actions.

docs.title: Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery
docs.text:
• BCP & DR Policy Must be in place and tested regularly.
  • Operational Resilience IT systems should support uninterrupted services during disruptions.

docs.title: Information Systems Audit
docs.text:
• IS Audit Must be conducted independently and cover all critical systems.
  • Audit Frequency Should align with risk profile and regulatory expectations.

Explore the official document RBI’s Master Directions page

Other key Financial regulations

docs.title: SEBI Cybersecurity & Cyber Resilience Framework (CSCRF)
docs.text:
• The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) regulates key market intermediaries
  • Applies to: Stock exchanges, Stock brokers, Asset Management Companies (AMC), KYC Registration Agencies (KRA), Credit Rating Agencies (CRA), Alternative Investment Funds (AIF)
  • Key Provisions: Create a single, risk-based cybersecurity and resilience baseline across the securities market, strengthening governance, incident response, third-party oversight, and continuous monitoring (SOC).
  • Penalties: SEBI directions, suspension, fines under SEBI Act

docs.title: IRDAI Cybersecurity Guidelines, 2023
docs.text:
• Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) regulates insurance sector
  • Applies to: Insurers and a broad ecosystem of intermediaries (e.g., brokers, web aggregators, repositories, surveyors, information bureau, Insurance Self Network Platform)
  • Key Provisions: Mandate an enterprise-wide ISMS with board oversight, documented cyber policies, CISO appointment, periodic risk assessments, incident response, and continuous assurance to reduce fraud and protect policyholder data.
  • Penalties: IT Act-linked liabilities and IRDAI enforcement actions

docs.title: Types of risk
docs.text:
• Inherent risk is the baseline level of risk exposure in an IT system, process, or asset before any security controls or mitigations are applied. It reflects the natural vulnerability due to factors like asset sensitivity, threat landscape, and operational complexity.

  • Residual risk is the level of risk that remains after all security controls, treatments, and mitigations have been applied to the original inherent risk. It represents the unavoidable exposure your organization accepts.

docs.title: Risk Appetite
docs.text:
• Risk appetite is the broad, strategic amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue to achieve objectives, often set by the board (e.g., high for growth-focused firms, low for conservative ones).

  • Risk tolerance defines the specific, measurable variation or deviation from objectives that the organization can withstand within that appetite, like operational limits or thresholds.

docs.title: Risk Acceptance
docs.text:
• Risk acceptance criteria are documented thresholds (for impact, likelihood, or overall risk rating) that define when a risk may be accepted rather than reduced, transferred, or avoided. They are aligned with the organization’s risk appetite (how much risk it is willing to take) and risk tolerance (how much variation from objectives it can withstand).
  • Risk acceptance is the tactical decision to formally approve and live with a specific risk that falls within tolerance after assessment, typically for residual risks post-mitigation.
  • The logic requires reducing risks until additional mitigation measures provide diminishing returns that are grossly disproportionate to their benefits. Risks fall into three zones on a typical risk matrix: unacceptable (must reduce regardless of cost), broadly acceptable (no action needed), and tolerable only if ALARP—meaning further controls are justified only if reasonably practicable

⚖️

ALARP stands for "As Low As Reasonably Practicable," while ALARA means "As Low As Reasonably Achievable." These are risk management principles used to balance safety or compliance benefits against the costs, time, and effort of further risk reduction.

To understand the IT Risk Management process, checkout ITRM

docs.title: 1. Identify Assets
docs.text: Determine the scope and identify where risks may exist within the organization. You can’t protect what you don’t know, so the first step is to create an inventory of all physical and logical assets.

docs.title: Key Asset Types
docs.text:
When identifying assets, it’s important to include: - Crown jewels – critical business assets that are prime targets for attackers. - Pivot assets – systems attackers may exploit to expand their reach (e.g., Active Directory servers, PACS).

Creating a network architecture diagram from the asset inventory helps visualize interconnectivity, communication paths, and entry points into the network.

docs.title: 2. Identify Risks
docs.text: Identify vulnerabilities, threats, and their potential impact. Threat actors use TTPs (tactics, techniques, procedures) that can compromise the CIA triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability).

docs.title: Resources
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK Knowledge Base
  • Cyber Threat Alliance
  • Security vendor reports and government advisories (e.g., CISA's KEV)

docs.title: 3. Assess the Risk
docs.text:
Evaluate the likelihood of each risk scenario and its potential impact.

Formula: Risk Level = Likelihood × Impact - Likelihood = Vulnerability × Threat - Impact = Effect on CIA triad

  • Likelihood: The probability that a threat can exploit a vulnerability. This should be based on discoverability, exploitability, and reproducibility, not just historical data (since cyber threats evolve rapidly).
  • Impact: The magnitude of harm if a vulnerability is exploited. Assess confidentiality, integrity, and availability separately, and use the highest rating as the final score.

docs.title: 3.1 Quantitative Risk Assessment (QRA)
docs.text:
Assigns monetary value to assets and calculates dollar cost of risk.

  • SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) = Asset Value × Exposure Factor
  • ARO (Annual Rate of Occurrence) = Frequency of event per year
  • ALE (Annual Loss Expectancy) = SLE × ARO

Example: - Asset Value = $500 - Exposure Factor = 50% → SLE = $250 - ARO = 4 → ALE = $250 × 4 = $1,000

docs.title: 3.2 Qualitative Risk Assessment
docs.text:
Evaluates risks using descriptive scales.

Scoring Example: - Likelihood: 1 (Rare) → 3 (Highly Likely) - Impact: 1 (Minor) → 3 (Severe)

docs.title: Risk Matrix
docs.text:
Impact ↓ / Likelihood → 1: Rare 2: Likely 3: Highly Likely 3: Severe High High Critical 2: Moderate Low High High 1: Minor Low Medium High

Risk Levels: - Low = Acceptable, monitor only - Medium = Requires mitigation planning - High = Needs prompt action - Critical = Immediate action required

docs.title: 3.3 Semi-Quantitative Approach
docs.text:
• A single incident causing >2% of annual earning or >X hours of outage is unacceptable.
  • Below those bands, acceptance may be considered subject to ALARP and management sign-off.

docs.title: 4. Prioritize Risks
docs.text: Rank identified risks based on severity. Helps determine which risks require immediate attention.

docs.title: 5. Risk Treatment
docs.text:
Decide how to handle each risk.

  • Avoid / Terminate – Discontinue activity to eliminate exposure. If the cost outweighs the benefit i.e. when risk exposure is unacceptable and easily preventable, discontinue the activity to eliminate exposure. This can be determined through quantitative or qualitative assessment.
  • Transfer – Shift liability (e.g., cyber insurance, outsourcing cloud security). Opt for transfer in high-impact scenarios where third parties can assume liability, such as cyber insurance for ransomware attacks or outsourcing cloud security to AWS/Azure managed services with SLAs (e.g., outsourcing DDoS mitigation, purchasing cyber insurance).
    • First-party coverage: Direct costs (e.g., breach notifications).
    • Third-party coverage: Settlements, penalties, fines.
    • Not covered: Intangible losses (IP theft, brand damage).
  • Mitigate – Implement security controls to reduce likelihood/impact. Ideal when treatment costs are justified.
  • Tolerate / Accept – Accept if risk falls within the organization’s risk acceptance criteria.

To read more about IT risk, checkout the article Risk Concepts

docs.title: 6. Communication
docs.text:
• Decisions must be communicated across the organization.
  • Stakeholders should understand costs of treating vs. not treating risks.
  • Roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined.

docs.title: 7. Rinse and Repeat
docs.text: Risk management is a continuous process. - Controls must be monitored and updated as systems evolve. - Regular reassessment ensures controls remain effective.

docs.title: RBI Directive
docs.text:
In April 2018, the RBI issued directive DPSS.CO.OD.No 2785/06.08.005/2017-18 requiring all payment system providers to store transaction data exclusively within India.

This applies to fintech firms, banks, and payment gateways processing transactions involving Indian citizens.

  • Mandate: Grants RBI unrestricted access to payment data for supervision, ensuring transparency and security.
  • Non-compliance: Can result in penalties, operational restrictions, or loss of licensure.

docs.title: Understanding the System Audit Report
docs.text: A SAR is a formal document submitted to the RBI, certifying compliance with data localization requirements. It involves a thorough assessment of IT infrastructure, data storage practices, and security controls.

docs.title: Key Aspects
docs.text:
1. CERT-In Empaneled Auditors – Audit must be conducted by auditors certified by CERT-In.
  2. Board Approval – Final report requires endorsement from the organization’s board.
  3. Comprehensive Documentation – Covers data classification, transaction flows, network architecture, access controls, and incident management protocols.

docs.title: Key Compliance Requirements
docs.text:
Organizations must demonstrate adherence to 17 critical domains outlined by RBI and NPCI, including:

  1. Payment Data Elements – Classify transaction details (e.g., card numbers, customer IDs) and ensure localized storage.
  2. Transaction Flow Mapping – Visualize end-to-end data movement, distinguishing between data at rest and in motion.
  3. Application Architecture – Provide diagrams of servers, databases, and APIs involved in payment processing.
  4. Data Security – Implement encryption, masking, and access controls.
  5. Disaster Recovery – Validate backup policies and restoration capabilities.
  6. Third-Party Risk Management – Assess vendor contracts and outsourcing risks.
  7. Fraud Risk Management – Controls to detect and prevent fraudulent transactions.
  8. Data Localization & Privacy – Storing payment data exclusively within India.

docs.title: Phase 1: Information Gathering & Documentation Review
docs.text:
• Auditors collect policies, architecture diagrams, and data flow charts.
  • Questionnaire aligned with RBI guidelines identifies gaps in controls.

docs.title: Phase 2: Assessment & Validation
docs.text:
• Technical controls tested against industry standards (e.g., encryption protocols).
  • Data storage locations and access logs verified for localization.

docs.title: Phase 3: Remediation & Re-Validation
docs.text:
• Organizations address vulnerabilities (e.g., unsecured APIs, cross-border data access).
  • Auditors re-test systems to confirm fixes.

docs.title: Phase 4: Certification & Submission
docs.text:
• CERT-In auditors issue compliance certificate.
  • Board-approved SAR submitted to RBI.

docs.title: Benefits of SAR Compliance
docs.text:
• Data Sovereignty – Protects citizen data from foreign surveillance during geopolitical conflicts.
  • Anti-Money Laundering (AML) – Detects suspicious transactions, strengthening global AML efforts.
  • Enhanced IT Governance – Identifies weaknesses in access management and network security.
  • Regulatory Trust – Demonstrates adherence to RBI norms, reducing legal risks.
  • Operational Resilience – Ensures robust disaster recovery and incident response plans.
