docs.title: SOC 1
docs.text:
• SOC 1 (System and Organization Controls Report) is an independent audit report on a service organization’s controls relevant to ICFR.
  • It is used by public companies and their auditors to evaluate outsourced services that impact financial reporting.

SOC 1 reports are critical for SOX compliance. If you’re new to SOX, checkout SOX overview

docs.title: SOC 1 Report Types
docs.text:
• Type 1: Describes the design of controls at a point in time
  • Type 2: Tests operating effectiveness of controls over a period — most relevant for SOX compliance

docs.title: Why SOX Compliance Is Reported in SOC 1
docs.text:
1. Scope Alignment

    • SOC 1 reports assess controls that affect financial reporting — exactly what SOX requires

  2. Third-Party Reliance

    • Companies often outsource critical processes (e.g., payroll, IT hosting, transaction processing)
    • SOC 1 reports provide assurance without re-auditing each vendor

  3. Audit Efficiency

    • SOC 1 reports are performed by independent service auditors
    • External auditors of public companies can rely on these reports, reducing duplication and cost

  4. Assurance Quality

    • SOC 1 reports provide auditor-grade assurance about third-party controls
    • They support SOX Section 404 compliance by demonstrating both the existence and effectiveness of relevant controls

docs.title: How SSAE 18 Supports SOX Compliance
docs.text:
• SOC 1 reports issued under SSAE 18 serve as trusted evidence for SOX Section 404 compliance
  • They allow public companies to rely on standardized, independent audits of their vendors — instead of conducting their own

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The report is created and validated by third-party auditors, which is built to provide independent assurance and verify that an organization is following specific best practices for business functions outsourced.

SOC 2 reporting is based on SSAE 18 attestation standard which is a general framework for CPAs (Certified Public Accountants) to perform attestation engagements — where an independent auditor examines and reports on subject matter other than traditional financial statements.

SSAE 18 (in 2017) which has superseded the AT 101 (previous standard), but the concepts from AT 101 still underpin SOC 2 reporting. AT 101 was not industry-specific framework (financial & non-financial) but it could be used for security, privacy, compliance, or other assurance topics.

The SOC 2 controls are not fixed checklist because the framework is principles-based (COSO) rather than prescriptive. Controls are derived from the five Trust Services Criteria (TSC), which are defined by the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA).

The 5 Trust Services criterias

Security, Availability, Processing integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy. Security controls testing is mandatory, while the rest (availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy) are optional.

Report Type

  • Type I: Design of controls at a specific point in time.

  • Type II: Design and operating effectiveness of controls over a period (typically 6–12 months).

docs.title: Service Auditor
docs.text:
• An independent CPA firm or audit professional who performs the SOC 2 examination.

  • They assess whether the service organization’s controls meet the Trust Services Criteria. They issue the final SOC 2 report, which includes their opinion on the design and/or operating effectiveness of control.

docs.title: Service Organization
docs.text:
• This is the company being audited in a SOC 2 report.

  • It provides services to other businesses (user entities), often involving data processing, cloud hosting, SaaS platforms, or IT infrastructure.

docs.title: Sub-Service Organization
docs.text:
• A third-party vendor that the service organization relies on to deliver part of its service.

  • Example: A SaaS company using AWS for cloud hosting — AWS is the sub-service organization.

There are two ways sub-service organization are handled in SOC 2:

  • Inclusive Method: Their controls are included and tested in the SOC 2 report.

  • Carve-Out Method: Their controls are excluded, but the service organization must describe what’s outsourced and what risks are involved.

docs.title: User Entity
docs.text:
• A client or customer of the service organization.

  • They rely on the service organization’s systems and controls to protect their data and operations.

  • Example: A bank using a third-party document management system.

docs.title: CUECs (Complementary User Entity Controls)
docs.text:
• These are controls that the user entity is responsible for.

  • The service organization assumes these controls are in place at the user entity to ensure the overall system works securely.

  • Example: If a service organization provides secure file sharing, the user entity must revoke access for terminated employees — the service organization on its own.

SOC 2 reports list CUECs so user entities know what they must do to uphold the shared security model.

docs.title: Report Components
docs.text: A SOC 2 report has five main parts, focusing on an organization's security controls related to one or more of the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. The sections provide details on the management's view of the audit, the auditor's official opinion, a description of the system under review, the testing results, and other information.

docs.title: Section I: Management's assertion
docs.text:
This section is drafted by the audited organization's management and outlines:

  • A summary of the services and systems covered by the audit.

  • A formal statement that the system description is presented fairly and that the controls were suitably designed.

  • A declaration of the service commitments and requirements addressed in the report.

  • Confirmation that management provided all relevant information to the auditor.

docs.title: Section II: Independent Service Auditor's report
docs.text:
This is the auditor's summary and opinion on the audit and is often the most important section for users of the report. It includes:

  • The scope and timeframe of the audit.

  • A description of the responsibilities of both management and the auditor.

  • The auditor's opinion: The final grade on the audit. Opinions can be:

    • Unqualified: The highest assurance, meaning controls are designed and operating effectively.

    • Qualified: Indicates that the controls have some deficiencies but are generally effective.

    • Adverse: A failure of the audit, indicating that controls are not effective and the system is unreliable.

    • Disclaimer of Opinion: The auditor was unable to form an opinion due to a lack of evidence.

docs.title: Section III: System description
docs.text:
This part, written by the service organization, provides a detailed overview of the system being audited. It is often the longest section and typically includes:

  • System components: The infrastructure, software, procedures, people, and data that are part of the system.

  • System boundaries: What is and is not included in the audit's scope.

  • Incidents and changes: Any system incidents or significant changes that occurred during the audit period.

  • Controls and processes: An explanation of the relevant security policies, risk management, and procedures.

docs.title: Section IV: Applicable Trust Services Criteria and test results
docs.text:
This section details how the organization addresses each of the applicable Trust Services Criteria (TSC).

  • Trust Services Criteria: All SOC 2 audits must cover the Security criterion, with other TSCs like Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, and Privacy being optional.

  • Controls and tests: It lists the controls put in place by the organization for each criterion, the test procedures the auditor performed, and the results of that testing. For a Type 2 report, this section also shows whether the controls operated effectively over time and notes any exceptions.

docs.title: Section V: Other information (optional)
docs.text:
In this final, non-audited section, management can provide additional context. It may be used to:

  • Explain the company's response to any exceptions or issues found by the auditor.

  • Detail future plans for system improvements.

  • Offer additional details about the company's control environment.

docs.title: SOC 3:
docs.text:
• A public-facing version of a SOC 2 Type II that does not include confidential information.

  • Provides a high-level summary for general customers without compromising or revealing details on the internal controls.

  • Usually only utilized by organizations that have conducted many SOC reports in the past and have a robust and mature control environment.

docs.title: SOC 1 vs SOC 2 vs SOC 3
docs.text: Feature / Aspect SOC 1 SOC 2 SOC 3 Primary Purpose Focuses on controls relevant to financial reporting (ICFR) for user entities’ auditors Focuses on controls relevant to Trust Services Criteria: Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy Same scope as SOC 2 but for general public consumption — high-level summary without detailed control/test results Typical Audience User entity management, user auditors (CPA firms), regulators Customers, prospects, business partners, internal risk teams Public stakeholders, marketing use, website posting Standard Used SSAE 18 (previously SSAE 16) — attestation standard for financial reporting controls Historically AT 101 (Attestation Standards Section 101), now under SSAE 18 — attestation standard for non-financial controls Same as SOC 2 (AT 101 → SSAE 18) but report omits sensitive details Criteria Management’s description of controls + control objectives relevant to financial reporting AICPA Trust Services Criteria (TSC) — based on COSO principles Same TSC as SOC 2 Report Types Type I (design at a point in time) and Type II (design + operating effectiveness over a period) Type I and Type II Only one format — general use summary Level of Detail Detailed control descriptions, tests, and results Detailed control descriptions, tests, and results High-level — no test results or sensitive details Confidentiality Restricted use Restricted use General use — can be shared publicly Common Use Case SOX 404 compliance evidence for outsourced processes Vendor due diligence for security/privacy; regulatory or contractual assurance Marketing proof of security posture without revealing sensitive details

docs.title: Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX), 2002
docs.text: The Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX) is a U.S. federal law that reshaped corporate governance and financial reporting after a wave of high-profile accounting scandals such as Enron, WorldCom, and Tyco.

docs.title: What It Is
docs.text:
• Applies to: All publicly traded companies in the U.S., their subsidiaries, and foreign companies listed on U.S. exchanges
  • Enforced by: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB)

docs.title: Purpose of SOX
docs.text:
The Act’s primary goals are to:

  1. Protect investors from fraudulent financial reporting
  2. Increase corporate accountability by holding executives personally responsible for the accuracy of financial statements
  3. Improve transparency in financial disclosures
  4. Strengthen internal controls over financial reporting
  5. Restore public trust in the integrity of the financial markets

In short:

  • Establish and maintain effective internal controls over financial reporting (ICFR)
  • Have those controls audited annually by an independent auditor (SOX Section 404)

docs.title: Five Key Provisions
docs.text: Section Focus Summary 302 Corporate Responsibility for Financial Reports CEO & CFO must personally certify the accuracy of financial statements and internal controls 401 Accurate Disclosures in Periodic Reports Financial statements must be accurate (adhering GAAP) and include all material off-balance sheet items 404 Management Assessment of Internal Controls Annual report must include management’s assessment of internal controls, verified by external auditors 409 Real-Time Issue Disclosures Companies must disclose material changes in financial condition promptly 802 Criminal Penalties for Altering Documents Severe penalties for destroying or falsifying records during investigations

docs.title: What’s Done to Comply
docs.text:
SOX compliance is an ongoing program, not a one-time project. Typical steps include:

  1. Establish Robust Internal Controls

    • Document all financial processes
    • Implement controls to prevent and detect errors or fraud
    • Use segregation of duties to reduce risk

  2. Management Certification

    • CEOs and CFOs must sign off on the accuracy of financial reports and the effectiveness of controls

  3. Independent External Audit

    • Annual audits by PCAOB-registered firms to verify financial statements and internal controls

  4. Continuous Monitoring

    • Regular internal audits and control testing
    • Real-time monitoring of financial transactions

  5. Record Retention Policies

    • Maintain financial records and audit trails for at least 7 years

  6. Whistleblower Protections

    • Establish confidential channels for reporting unethical or illegal activities

  7. Penalties for Non-Compliance ⚠️

    • Civil penalties: Heavy fines for companies and executives
    • Criminal penalties: Up to 20 years in prison for willful violations such as securities fraud or document destruction

SOX Section 404 compliance often relies on SOC 1 reports, see SOC1 overview.

docs.title: SWIFT – Secure Financial Messaging
docs.text:
• SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication) is the global network that enables banks and financial institutions to exchange standardized, secure financial messages (e.g., payment instructions, securities trades, FX confirmations).

  • It doesn’t move money itself; it transmits the instructions that allow institutions to settle transactions.

docs.title: SWIFT CSP – Customer Security Programme
docs.text:
• What it is: A cybersecurity initiative launched in 2016 after high-profile fraud incidents.

  • Purpose: To strengthen the overall security of the SWIFT ecosystem by ensuring that member institutions protect their local environments (not just the central SWIFT network).

  • Scope: Covers governance, risk management, and operational security practices for all SWIFT users.

  • Requirement: Institutions must self-attest annually to their compliance with CSP standards, and some must undergo independent assessments.

docs.title: CSCF – Customer Security Controls Framework
docs.text:
The SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework (CSCF) is part of the SWIFT Customer Security Programme (CSP). It was developed by the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) to strengthen cybersecurity across its global financial messaging network.

Who Governs It?

  • Governing Body: The CSP is governed by SWIFT (Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication), a member-owned cooperative headquartered in Belgium.

  • Oversight: SWIFT’s Board of Directors and cybersecurity teams oversee the development and enforcement of the CSP and CSCF.

  • Compliance: Institutions must self-attest annually to their compliance, and some are required to undergo independent assessments.

Where Is It Applicable?

The CSP applies to all institutions that use the SWIFT network, including: Banks, Brokerages, Clearing houses, Payment service providers, Central banks.

It is globally applicable, covering over 11,000 institutions in more than 200 countries. Whether a small regional bank or a multinational financial giant, any entity connected to SWIFT must comply with the CSCF controls.

docs.title: Objectives
docs.text:
The CSCF is structured around three overarching objectives:

  1. Secure your environment – Protect the local SWIFT infrastructure.

  2. Know and limit access – Control who and what can access SWIFT systems.

  3. Detect and respond – Monitor for suspicious activity and respond to incidents.

These objectives are supported by 8 core principles and 32 detailed security controls.

Key Components:

  • Mandatory Controls: These are baseline security requirements that all SWIFT users must implement. They cover areas like access control, malware protection, and secure communication.

  • Advisory Controls: These are best practices that SWIFT recommends but does not require. They help institutions go beyond the minimum and improve their overall security posture.

docs.title: Control List
docs.text:
The SWIFT Customer Security Controls Framework (CSCF) includes 32 controls—20 mandatory and 12 advisories—organized under 8 security principles to protect institutions using the SWIFT network.

  1. Restrict Internet Access

    1.1. No direct internet access to SWIFT systems (Mandatory)

    1.2. Operating system privileged account control (Mandatory)

    1.3A. Secure internet access points (Advisory)

  2. Protect Critical Systems from General IT Environment

    2.1. Segregate SWIFT systems from general IT (Mandatory)

    2.2. Reduce shared use of SWIFT components (Mandatory)

    2.3A. Protect SWIFT components from malware (Advisory)

    2.4. Application whitelisting (Mandatory)

  3. Reduce Attack Surface and Vulnerabilities

    3.1. Timely application of security updates (Mandatory)

    3.2. System hardening (Mandatory)

    3.3A. Remove unnecessary software/services (Advisory)

  4. Physically Secure the Environment

    4.1. Restrict physical access (Mandatory)

    4.2. multi-factor authentication (Mandatory)

    4.3A. Monitor physical access (Advisory)

  5. Prevent Compromise of Credentials

    5.1. Logical access control (Mandatory)

    5.2. Password policy enforcement (Mandatory)

    5.3A. Privileged access management (Advisory)

  6. Detect and Respond to Anomalies

    6.1. Logging and monitoring (Mandatory)

    6.2. Detect anomalous activity (Mandatory)

    6.3A. Centralized log collection (Advisory)

    6.4A. Behavioural monitoring (Advisory)

    6.5A. Intrusion detection (Advisory)

  7. Plan for Incident Response and Information Sharing

    7.1. Cyber incident response plan (Mandatory)

    7.2A. Information sharing with SWIFT community (Advisory)

  8. Ensure Integrity of Software and Data

    8.1. Software integrity validation (Mandatory)

    8.2. Database integrity checks (Mandatory)

    8.3A. Cryptographic file validation (Advisory)

    8.4A. Secure backup and recovery (Advisory)

docs.title: Why It Matters for Compliance
docs.text:
Any institution using the SWIFT network must demonstrate compliance with the CSCF. This includes:

• Annual self-attestation of compliance status.

• Independent assessments (mandatory for some users).

• Ongoing updates as the framework evolves to address emerging threats.

Non-compliance can lead to reputational damage, regulatory scrutiny, or even restricted access to the SWIFT network.

docs.title: RBI's Recognition and Oversight of SWIFT
docs.text:
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has officially recognized SWIFT and mandated Indian banks to comply with its security standards. RBI has issued guidelines and taken enforcement actions to ensure SWIFT-related operational controls are implemented across Indian financial institutions.

  • Official Recognition: RBI acknowledges SWIFT as a critical infrastructure for international financial messaging and has issued multiple circulars since 2016 to strengthen its security environment in Indian banks.

  • Compliance Mandate: RBI requires all banks using SWIFT to implement specific operational and cybersecurity controls, aligned with SWIFT’s Customer Security Controls Framework (CSCF).

  • Monitoring and Enforcement: RBI monitors compliance through inspections and has imposed penalties on banks failing to meet SWIFT-related requirements.

docs.title: Unified Payments Interface's - Information Security Compliance Framework 2025
Purpose & Objective
docs.text:
• Issued by NPCI to standardize UPI security across all participants.
  • Ensures confidentiality, integrity, availability, privacy, and resilience in payment applications.
  • Requires proactive risk recognition and mitigation for cybersecurity and emerging technologies

docs.title: NPCI
docs.text: National Payments Corporation of India is the umbrella organization that manages India’s retail payment and settlement systems. Its role is to design, operate, and regulate digital payment infrastructure like UPI, RuPay, IMPS, and BHIM, ensuring secure, efficient, and inclusive payment services across the country.

docs.title: Applicability
docs.text: Covers banks (remitter, issuer, acquiring), prepaid instrument issuers, third-party app providers (TPAPs), technology service providers, voice-based service providers, IVR providers, and application service providers.

docs.title: Framework components
docs.text:
• Governance Controls: Clear policies, CISO accountability, board oversight, compliance monitoring.
  • Security Measures: Identity & access management, fraud risk controls, data privacy, network & infrastructure security, application lifecycle security, incident response, API security.
  • Operational Review: Business continuity planning, disaster recovery drills, VAPT testing, logging & monitoring, architecture reviews.

docs.title: Key Compliance Enforced
docs.text:
1.Annual Security Audits

  • Mandatory Audits All banks, Payment Service Providers (PSPs), and Third‑Party App Providers (TPAPs) must undergo annual audits by CERT‑In empanelled auditors.

  • Scope Audits cover infrastructure, applications, APIs, and operational processes.

  • Pre‑Onboarding New participants must complete audits before joining UPI or other NPCI systems.

2. Vulnerability Remediation

  • Fix Before Reporting Entities must remediate all identified vulnerabilities before submitting compliance reports.

  • No Pending High‑Risk Issues Remediation must be verified by auditors.

  • Continuous Practices Patch management and secure coding are enforced continuously.

3. UPI API Security Guidelines (OC‑215, 2025 Update)

  • Mandate NPCI requires secure API design and deployment for UPI participants.

  • Requirements Include:

    • Strong authentication and authorization protocols
    • Encryption of data in transit and at rest
    • Rate limiting and monitoring to prevent abuse
    • Secure key management and tokenization

  • Purpose Ensures PSPs, banks, and TPAPs maintain resilient and scalable API interactions.

4. Data Protection & Localization

  • Storage in India Payment transaction data must be stored only in India, per RBI and NPCI directives.

  • Privacy & Backups Entities must comply with data privacy frameworks and ensure secure backups.

  • Access Controls Sensitive data access is restricted and logged.

5. Incident Reporting & Monitoring

  • Reporting Timeline Any security breach or incident must be reported to NPCI within 24 hours.

  • Fraud Monitoring Participants must maintain real‑time fraud monitoring systems.

  • Log Preservation Transaction and system activity logs must be preserved for forensic analysis., per RBI and NPCI directives.

6. Compliance Frameworks

  • UPI Information Security & Compliance Framework 2025 Sets standardized rules for all stakeholders.

  • Emphasis On:

    • Continuous compliance
    • Risk‑based approach to security
